commits.subject: docs(backlog): record the util.inspect and toLocaleString gaps
commits.body:
Both surfaced while building the verbatim Rosetta suite, which runs
unmodified third-party code and so reaches host surfaces our own tests never
touch.

util.inspect is the larger of the two and is not confined to plain objects:
arrays lose their brackets, Map/Set render as [object Map], functions do not
get [Function: f], and a cyclic structure would need [Circular *1]. The
console format-specifier machinery beside it is complete and verified against
node, so this is the one piece missing from that file.

toLocaleString is filed as a gap rather than out of scope deliberately. The
Out of scope list excludes the intl402 *test suite*; it does not say the
method may ignore its arguments. Today's fallback to toString() is conformant
under ES5 15.9.5.5, which is why it is not a bug — but it is still a hole
against ECMA-402 and it cost the suite a sample.

commits.subject: test: drive verbatim samples by concatenation, not ESM
commits.body:
The suite ran check files through --module, relying on the engine exposing
unexported top-level bindings so an unmodified sample could be imported. That
was a conformance gap, and f7fd26ce fixed it: ECMA-262 16.2.1.6.3 makes an
unresolvable import a link-time SyntaxError. 27 of the 41 tests broke on rebase,
exactly as the previous commit message predicted.

The fix is correct and stays. The suite was wrong to depend on it: these samples
are plain scripts with no export statements, and adding any would break the
byte-identity with the wiki that is the entire point. run.sh now concatenates
harness + sample + check into one script -- which is how the samples were
written to run, with all top-level declarations sharing one scope.

Dropped assertImported. It existed only to turn a silently-undefined import into
a loud failure; with concatenation a missing binding is a plain ReferenceError
on first use, which is louder still (verified by renaming gcd's function and
confirming "Uncaught: gcd is not defined"). The vestigial import lines in check
files became "// Drives <sample>.js" comments -- run.sh no longer strips them,
and leaving them implied a module relationship that does not exist.

No sample file changed; the drift check against rosettacode.org still passes.
Re-ran the mutation sweep against the new mechanism: 31 caught, 8 unmutatable,
and the same 2 previously-proven-equivalent mutations, matching the pre-rebase
numbers exactly.

commits.subject: test: expand verbatim Rosetta suite to 41 samples
commits.body:
Extends the 10-task pilot across every task the old test/rosetta/ suite cited.
28 samples are driven by assertion files, 13 by comparing printed output.

Expected outputs are cross-checked against QuickJS rather than recorded only
from our own engine -- a .expected generated from our output alone would pass
even if the engine were wrong. All 13 output files and all 28 assertion files
agree with qjs.

Mutation-tested end to end: a fault injected into each sample must fail its
check. 31 caught, 8 samples have no numeric literal or comparison to perturb,
and the 2 apparent misses were verified equivalent by exhaustive search -- gcd's
`b > a` vs `b >= a` differs only when a === b (swapping equal values is a no-op)
and quicksort's `left < right` vs `left <= right` only adds a no-op recursive
call. The sweep found three real coverage holes, now fixed: a sieve boundary at
limit == 2, a stack check that could not observe the pushed values, and a
fizzbuzz check that restated the sample's rules instead of capturing its output.

Two engine gaps found and deliberately not worked around; the samples that
depend on them were excluded instead:

- Date.prototype.toLocaleString ignores its options bag and timeZone, returning
  a default date string in local time (ECMA-402). Excludes the Date_format task.
- console.log does not inspect objects (prints "[object Object]") and does not
  substitute %d/%s format specifiers. Both are Node behaviors, not spec.

Also worth recording: 22 of the URLs the old suite cited point at wiki pages
that do not exist, which is further evidence those attributions were invented
rather than followed.

fetch_rosetta.py gained shebang handling (a provenance header cannot precede
`#!`, which is only honored on line 1) and a clean error on a failed fetch.

commits.subject: test: add verbatim Rosetta Code suite
commits.body:
Ten JavaScript samples copied byte-identically from rosettacode.org, run
unmodified so the engine is exercised by third-party code we did not write.
This is the signal test/engine/ cannot give: those tests are ours, so they only
cover constructs we thought to use.

Samples never carry assertions. Each <name>.js is driven either by a
<name>.check.js that imports it (via the --module ESM path) or, when the
sample's behavior is what it prints, by diffing stdout against <name>.expected.
scripts/fetch_rosetta.py fetches samples and, with --check, re-fetches from the
wiki to confirm no local copy has drifted.

Every sample was mutation-tested: a deliberate fault injected into each one is
caught by its check file. That pass found a real coverage hole -- all five gcd
inputs exited through the same loop branch, so a fault in the other branch went
undetected. Added divisor-pair cases that reach it.

Two engine behaviors this suite depends on, both worth noting:

- Top-level var/function bindings are importable without an export statement.
  Real ESM requires explicit exports; this deviation is what makes importing an
  unmodified sample possible at all.
- An unresolvable import name yields undefined instead of failing to link, so a
  renamed sample function would silently assert against undefined and pass.
  ES2015 s15.2.1.16.3 ResolveExport makes that an early SyntaxError. Every check
  file calls assertImported() first to turn it into a loud failure, but the gap
  itself should be fixed separately.

commits.subject: test: rename test/rosetta to test/engine and fix workarounds
commits.body:
These 100 files were never reproductions of Rosetta Code samples. Each cited a
rosettacode.org URL in its header but reimplemented the algorithm from scratch
in a local assert harness. Comparing five of them against the wiki source
(?action=raw) showed no shared code: the real String_interpolation sample is
three lines using String.replace, ours is a hand-rolled sprintf with a regex
callback; the real Ackermann is a one-line ternary; the real Roman_numerals uses
a flat map array, ours an array of pairs plus a decoder the Encode task does not
have.

Drop the misleading attribution and name the directory for what it is. Verbatim
samples now live in test/rosetta-verbatim/.

Also fix the workarounds the attribution was hiding:

- strict_mode.js dropped its duplicate-parameter test with a comment saying
  "this engine doesn't allow it", replacing it with add(2,3) === 5. The comment
  was wrong: duplicate params in strict code are a SyntaxError (ES5.1 s13.1),
  so rejecting them is correct. Restored as a real test through eval, along
  with the delete-unqualified-identifier rule its empty catch block skipped.
- roman_numerals.js and sum_series.js ended a verification loop with
  assert(true, ...), inflating the pass count with an unconditional assertion.
  Both now assert on a flag the loop sets.
- ackermann.js capped at ack(3,3) citing engine stack limits; ack(3,5) runs
  fine, so the cap is about runtime, not a limitation.
- random.js carried a defensive comment about a deviation; trimmed to the
  operative reason.

commits.subject: Merge arrow-body var hoisting, and a parameter-clobber it was masking
commits.body:
compile_arrow_inner never called hoist_decls, so an arrow's block body
hoisted no var at all: a var in an unexecuted branch was absent rather
than undefined. Both arrow paths now call it, mirroring
parse_function_body. Pattern support came free from 3c98e182.

A SECOND, PRE-EXISTING BUG SURFACED, and it affects ORDINARY FUNCTIONS
rather than arrows: hoist_one_var_name called declare_var
unconditionally, so a var re-declaring a PARAMETER allocated a fresh
register and LDUNDEF-ed it, destroying the argument.

  function f(p){ if (false) { var p = 1; } return p; }  f(7)
  gave undefined; node gives 7

Per ES2015 9.2.10 step 27 only var names absent from parameterNames get
the undefined initialisation. In arrows the two bugs had been
CANCELLING — the absent hoist could not clobber the param — so fixing
the hoist alone turned 11 differential cells newly wrong. Not separable.

The loud half of the arrow bug was the smaller half. Three cases fail
SILENTLY with plausible values:

  var n='outer'; (()=>{ if(false){var n=1;} return n; })()
  gave 'outer'; node gives undefined

264-cell differential vs node: 107 accept / 157 reject before, 264 / 0
after — every changed cell to node's exact value, not merely
"stopped throwing". test262 has ZERO coverage for any of this: 0 tests
gained. The accept table was the only thing that found it, which is now
eight consecutive tasks.

Phases 0/3/11/14/25 stay at zero failures; 21 and 24 carry their
pre-existing 3 and 5. Local 296 scripts, golden 28/28, both RSS guards
green. Arrow `this` and enclosing-`arguments` behaviour is byte-identical
to before. An empty file still runs — checked deliberately, since an
earlier attempt on the reparse path bricked the engine by consuming a
token during lookahead.

Expression-bodied arrows deliberately skip the hoist, since an
AssignmentExpression has no statement-level declarations; the reasoning
is recorded inline so it does not read as an oversight.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): an arrow's block body hoists its var declarations
commits.body:
compile_arrow_inner and compile_arrow_inner_reparse went straight from the
parameter list to statement compilation, so an arrow's block ConciseBody
never ran hoist_decls at all. A `var` in an unreached branch therefore
produced NO binding rather than an undefined one:

  (() => { if (false) { var x = 1; } return x; })()
    → ReferenceError "x is not defined", where node gives undefined

The equivalent `function` form was already correct, which is what confines
this to the arrow forms. A block ConciseBody is a FunctionBody, so its
VarDeclaredNames hoist exactly like an ordinary function's; both arrow
paths now mirror parse_function_body's ordering (pre-scan, hoist, pin).
Expression-bodied arrows deliberately do not hoist: an AssignmentExpression
has no statement-level declarations. is_global is false unconditionally,
propagating it would wrongly make arrow-body vars global (6c492b9c).

The throw is the loud half. The quiet half is that with no hoisted slot the
read resolved OUTWARD, so an arrow-body `var` failed to shadow an outer
binding of the same name and returned the enclosing value:

  var n = 'outer'; (() => { if (false) { var n = 1; } return n; })()
    → 'outer', where node gives undefined

Fixing that exposed a second, older bug in hoist_one_var_name, which
affected ordinary functions equally and is fixed here too: it called
declare_var unconditionally, allocating a FRESH register and emitting
LDUNDEF into it even when the name was already a PARAMETER, so the argument
value was lost. Per ES2015 §9.2.10 step 27 only var names ABSENT from
parameterNames get the undefined initialization.

  function f(p){ if (false) { var p = 1; } return p; }  f(7) → undefined

In arrows the two bugs cancelled (the absent hoist could not clobber the
param), so this only became visible once the first was fixed. New
is_param_name gates the skip on the scope entry's is_param flag rather than
plain name presence: at hoist time the only bindings in scope are the
parameters, but the narrower test survives that ceasing to hold.

264-cell differential vs node ({var in an unexecuted if, zero-iteration
for/while/for-in/for-of, after return, nested block, nested function,
nested arrow, binding patterns, param shadowing, outer shadowing,
initializer that runs, unmatched switch, labelled break, catch} x
{expression-bodied, block-bodied, async, in a function, in an arrow, method
value, IIFE, class field, defaulted params, rest, destructured param,
single-identifier param}): 107 accept / 157 reject before, 264 / 0 after,
zero newly broken. test262 phases 0-8, 11, 14, 21, 24, 25 comm-diffed
per-test against a baseline built at 82d340ba: 36238 pass / 8 fail on both,
0 previously-passing lost, 0 gained — the suite has no coverage for any of
this. Local 296 scripts, golden 28/28, both RSS guards green.

test/codegen_arrow_var_hoisting.js is 45/45 here and under node unmodified.
On the 82d340ba baseline the throwing cases exit 1; more importantly the
three silent wrong-VALUE cases (outer shadowing, enclosing-local shadowing,
parameter clobbering) fail there while returning plausible answers, which
is why nothing caught them. `arguments` still resolves to the enclosing
function's through any depth of arrows, `this` is still lexical, and the
arrow still creates no arguments object of its own.

commits.subject: Merge Annex B.3.9 citation for call-expression assignment targets
commits.body:
Documentation only — 52 comment lines, zero non-comment changes.

f() = 1 is an early SyntaxError here and a runtime ReferenceError in
node. I dispatched this expecting the usual answer: node is the lenient
outlier, we and QuickJS are right, close it with a citation. The
conclusion holds, but the reasoning I supplied was wrong.

A NORMATIVE ALLOWANCE FOR NODE'S BEHAVIOUR DOES EXIST. ES2025 8.6.4
AssignmentTargetType returns three values — simple, web-compat, invalid
— and the CallExpression clause is a Normative Optional returning
web-compat when the host supports Annex B.3.9 "Runtime Errors for
Function Call Assignment Targets" AND IsStrict is false.

It is unreachable in this engine, but only because of the strict-only
design: IsStrict is always true, so step 1 never fires, step 2 returns
invalid, and 13.15.1's early error applies. The early SyntaxError is
the ONLY spec-conforming outcome here — not the stricter of two
permitted readings. Had this engine supported sloppy mode, deferring to
runtime would have been correct.

Node is also not simply lenient. It gives SyntaxError for f() &&= 1 and
f() ??= 1 while giving ReferenceError for f() += 1, deliberately
implementing B.3.9's carve-out: the = and AssignmentOperator early-error
clauses test "is invalid" so web-compat suppresses them, while the
logical-assignment clause tests "is not simple" so web-compat is
rejected too. Verified against node and QuickJS.

Node does have a real deviation, in the opposite direction from the one
I assumed: it applies B.3.9 even in genuinely strict code, so f() = 1
in a .mjs module yields ReferenceError although the allowance is gated
on non-strict code. It therefore fails test262's onlyStrict
direct-callexpression.js, which we and QuickJS pass.

All 10 test262 tests citing the web-compat clause pass. Comment-only, so
inert by construction; test_assignment_target_type.js 252/252, golden
28/28, local 295 scripts, both RSS guards green.

commits.subject: docs(compiler): cite Annex B.3.9 for early-erroring call assignment targets
commits.body:
Records why `f() = 1`, `(f()) = 1` and `(f())++` stay early SyntaxErrors
here even though V8/node parse them and throw a runtime ReferenceError.

Unlike the other node divergences settled this session, the spec really
does sanction a deferral. AssignmentTargetType (ES2025 §8.6.4) returns
simple, web-compat or invalid, and the CallExpression clause is a
Normative Optional: if the host is a web browser or otherwise supports
Runtime Errors for Function Call Assignment Targets, and IsStrict(this
CallExpression) is false, return web-compat; otherwise return invalid.
Annex B.3.9 spells out the consequence — in non-strict code a
ReferenceError is thrown during evaluation instead of an early error.

The allowance is unreachable here because it is gated on IsStrict being
false and this engine is strict-only, so step 1 never fires, step 2
returns invalid, and §13.15.1's early error applies. The early
SyntaxError is the only spec-conforming outcome for this engine, not
merely the stricter of two permitted readings.

test262 covers this directly and agrees: all ten
language/expressions/assignmenttargettype/*callexpression* tests citing
the web-compat clause expect `phase: parse, type: SyntaxError`, and each
one whose operator is deferrable is flagged onlyStrict. The two
logical-assignment cases carry no strictness flag, matching B.3.9's Note
that the allowance never extends to `&&=`/`||=`/`??=` (whose §13.15.1
clause tests "is not simple", which rejects web-compat as well as
invalid). All ten pass.

node fits the same shape — deferring for `=`, `+=` and `++` but keeping a
SyntaxError for `&&=`/`??=` — so it is implementing B.3.9 rather than
being merely lenient; it just also applies it to genuinely strict code
(a `.mjs` module still yields ReferenceError), which B.3.9 does not
permit. QuickJS matches this engine on all twelve probes.

Behaviour is unchanged; this commit is the citation.

commits.subject: Merge the last early-error groups: parse-negative failures reach zero
commits.body:
Closes the programme a7c9fb95 opened. That commit un-skipped 4197
negative:phase:parse test262 tests and exposed 765 failures; six merges
later there are none. Phases 0-8, 11, 14 and 25 all report 0 fail.

Eight groups: ASI restricted productions ([no LineTerminator here] after
throw, and the yield/++ cases); the grammar's [~In] parameter for a
C-style for head; HTML-like comments restricted to Script, per 12.5;
both ModuleExportName early errors; ExportedBinding must be declared in
this module; unterminated comments and the two numeric-literal early
errors; three grammar-level singletons; and two over-rejections the
accept table caught.

THE 8 assignmenttargettype TESTS FELL OUT OF THIS WORK. They were being
handled separately as a register-allocator restructure (1bee8d12), and
both branches independently fixed the same defect. The rebase conflict
was resolved toward 1bee8d12's last_target_invalid, which is the broader
mechanism — it covers (x = y) = 1, (x ??= y)++ and more through a
wrapper — and the narrower last_was_assignment flag was dropped. Both
behaviours verified after resolution: the invalid targets reject,
(a) = 1 / (o.p) = 1 / (u = 45) > 0 still work, fib(10) = 55.

Two prerequisites fixed on the way, both real: pre_scan_var_decls
reported only the first declarator of any `var a = 1, b = 2`, and
test/test_octal_strict.js asserted 08 === 8, encoding the very bug the
non-octal-decimal-integer-strict tests exist to catch.

The Annex B question resolved opposite to how I framed it: the engine
already implemented HTML-like comments unconditionally, so restricting
them to Script was a REMOVAL, not an addition, and no skip was
warranted.

Node was the lenient outlier again on for (o.async of [1]), where
QuickJS and the grammar agree with us. The accept table caught three
over-rejections no failing test would have found, including a first
[no LT] fix that errored on `yield \n + 1` instead of letting ASI run.

Local 295 scripts, 101 module-syntax, 63 export-names; golden 28/28;
both RSS guards green.

commits.subject: fix: two over-rejections from the for-of and export-binding checks
commits.body:
Caught by the full phase 0-8/11/14/25 run, which reported 13 unexpected
compile errors where the baseline had none.

- for-of `async` head: the §14.7.5 lookahead excludes the literal TOKEN
  `async`, so an escaped spelling (`async`) is an ordinary
  IdentifierReference and is still a valid loop target
  (for-of/head-lhs-async-escaped). Gate on Token.has_escape.
- `export var { x } = o`: check_module_exports_resolvable derived declared
  names from a var pre-scan that stops at a non-identifier, so a destructuring
  declarator's leaf names were invisible and the export looked unresolvable.
  An `export`-PREFIXED declaration binds its own name in the same statement,
  so it satisfies §16.2.1.1 by construction; CompExportEntry.declares_binding
  records that and the check skips those entries instead of trying to
  reconstruct the leaves. This covered the 12 top-level-await
  export-var-await-expr-* tests, whose second line is exactly that shape.

Regression coverage: 4 more cases in test/modules/export_names.sh (59 -> 63)
and the escaped-async case in test/test_early_error_singletons.js (39 -> 40).

commits.subject: fix(parser): three early errors whose restriction lives in the grammar
commits.body:
Each of these was accepted because the rule is expressed as a production shape
rather than as anything the parser was checking.

- §13.15.1  An AssignmentExpression has AssignmentTargetType ~invalid~, so
  `(a = b) = 1` is a SyntaxError. The existing reference markers cannot carry
  this: parentheses deliberately PRESERVE AssignmentTargetType (`(a) = 1` is
  legal) and a compound assignment's result path sets last_was_local_var on
  purpose to drive the copy-to-temp guard for `(n *= 0.3) > 0`. Hence a
  separate last_was_assignment, cleared before each operand parse and re-armed
  after each of the four RHS parses, read by the invalid-LHS test.
- §14.3  A getter takes no parameter and a setter exactly one. A setter's
  PropertySetParameterList is a FormalParameter, not a FormalParameterList, so
  a rest parameter is not one of the forms it admits (node agrees; QuickJS
  accepts `set a(...r)`, which the grammar does not). Checked against the
  compiled inner function's num_args — num_formals is Function.length, which a
  default value reduces. Both the object-literal and class paths, via a shared
  AccessorKind. Beyond the reported getter case this also caught `set a()` and
  `set a(v, w)`, over-accepted the same way.
- §14.7.5  `for ( [lookahead ∉ { let [, async of }] LeftHandSideExpression of
  ... )`: the token pair `async of` is excluded at the head's start, so a
  variable named `async` needs parenthesizing. This is a 2-token lookahead at
  the START, so `for (o.async of [1])` stays legal — node rejects that one,
  QuickJS accepts it, and the grammar is on QuickJS's side.

test262: assignment/target-assignment, target-assignment-inside-function,
object/getter-param-dflt and for-of/head-lhs-async-invalid now pass (4 tests).
test/test_early_error_singletons.js is new: 39 cases, with the two
engine-divergent rows documented in its header.

commits.subject: fix(lexer): unterminated comments, and the two numeric-literal early errors
commits.body:
Three lexer-level rules, each of which was silently over-accepting:

- §12.4  A MultiLineComment must be closed. The scan broke out of its loop on
  end-of-input and returned EOF, so the source compiled as though it ended
  just before the `/*`. skip_whitespace_and_comments returns void and runs
  from several non-failing paths, so it latches `unterminated_comment` and
  next_token raises. This also covers `/*/`, where the `/` that looks like a
  closer is part of the opener.
- §12.9.3.1  BOTH `0`-led decimal integer forms are strict-mode Syntax Errors:
  LegacyOctalIntegerLiteral (`01`) and NonOctalDecimalIntegerLiteral (`08`).
  The guard tested for 0-7 only, so `08` and `09` were accepted. `0` followed
  by any decimal digit is one of the two, so one range covers both;
  `0x`/`0o`/`0b`/`0.`/`0e` are unaffected, their second character is not a
  decimal digit.
- §12.9.3  "The SourceCharacter immediately following a NumericLiteral must
  not be an IdentifierStart or DecimalDigit." `3in []` lexed as `3` then the
  `in` keyword and parsed happily; `3if` only failed because `if` cannot
  continue an expression.

record_lex_error names an unterminated comment instead of reporting whichever
byte precedes the lexer position, which for an EOF-terminated scan was
meaningless.

test262: comments/S7.4_A2_T2, literals/regexp/S7.8.5_A1.2_T1,
numeric/non-octal-decimal-integer-strict and numeric/numeric-followed-by-ident
now pass (4 tests).

test/test_octal_strict.js asserted `08 === 8` — it was encoding the bug. It
now asserts the rejection (node --check agrees) and gains the neighbouring
`0`-led literals plus the numeric-followed-by-identifier cases, 20 -> 33
assertions. test/test_comment_termination.js is new, 13 cases, identical
results under node.

commits.subject: fix(module): an ExportedBinding must be declared in this module
commits.body:
§16.2.1.1: every element of ExportedBindings must also occur in the
VarDeclaredNames or LexicallyDeclaredNames of the ModuleItemList. So
`export { unresolvable };` is a SyntaxError, and so is `export { Number };` —
a global is not a module-level declaration.

check_module_exports_resolvable runs after the whole body is parsed, because
the rule is about the item LIST: `export { later }; var later = 1;` is legal.
It reads the four places a module-level declared name can be by then: the
scope stack (let/const/class, hence the call before pop_scope_to), the hoisted
function names, the module's func_decls (an `export function g(){}` carries
its own prefix and the hoisting pre-scan never sees it), a var pre-scan (a
module-level `var` is never pushed to the scope stack), and the import
entries. Only local exports are checked: `export {x} from` names `x` in the
other module, and a star export names nothing here.

pre_scan_var_decls stopped at the first `=`, so `var a = 1, b = 2` reported
only `a`. It now skips the Initializer to the separating comma, tracking
nesting so a `,` inside `f(1, 2)` is not mistaken for one. Its existing caller
(check_lexical_var_conflicts) was unaffected in practice — the declaration-time
check_var_lex_conflict catches those pairs first — but the scan's contract is
every declarator, and this caller depends on it.

test262: module-code/early-export-global and early-export-unresolvable now
pass (2 tests). test/modules/export_names.sh gains 14 cases (45 -> 59), each
cross-checked against `node --check`.

commits.subject: fix(module): the two ModuleExportName early errors
commits.body:
§16.2.3.1 puts two restrictions on a StringLiteral ModuleExportName, neither
of which was enforced:

- It is a Syntax Error if IsStringWellFormedUnicode of its StringValue is
  false. A lone surrogate names an export no importer could ever spell.
  parse_module_export_name now rejects it, which covers every position at
  once: an export alias, a re-export, `export * as`, and an import name.
- `export NamedExports ;` with no `from` clause is a Syntax Error if
  ReferencedBindings contains a ModuleExportName. Without a `from` a
  specifier's local half names a binding in this module, and a string is not

commits.body:

commits.subject: fix(parser): implement the grammar's [~In] parameter for a C-style for head
commits.body:
`for ( Expression[~In] ; ... )` has no production for a top-level `in` — it
would be ambiguous with a for-in head (ES2024 §14.7.4). The parser had no In
parameter at all, so `for (1 in arr; 1;)` parsed as a for-in that then failed
on nothing, and both conditional-operand cases were accepted.

forbid_in follows the same consume-on-entry discipline as yield_ok_here:
binary_expr captures and clears it, so it governs exactly that invocation's
operator loop and can never leak into a nested construct. Parentheses,
brackets, call arguments and template substitutions are therefore `[+In]` for
free, whichever entry point they use, and `for (f(a in b);;)` stays legal.

Two sites re-fix the parameter by hand because their grammar does:
- conditional_expr holds it across the condition and hands `[+In]` to the
  middle operand but `[?In]` to the false one, so `for (a ? b in c : d;;)`
  is legal and `for (a ? b : c in d;;)` is not.
- a for head's declarator initializers are `[~In]`, so
  `for (var x = 1 in {};;)` is a SyntaxError (node agrees; the shape was
  accepted before).

`#x in o` is likewise `[+In]`-only, so it is unavailable in the head too.

commits.subject: fix(parser): enforce the [no LineTerminator here] restricted productions
commits.body:
`throw`, `=>` and `yield *` each carry a `[no LineTerminator here]` in their
grammar. None of them is an ASI opportunity — the construct has no shorter
form to fall back to — so a line break there is a SyntaxError, not a
silently-different parse.

- throw_statement: reject a line terminator between `throw` and its Expression
  (ES2024 §14.14). Previously `throw \n 1;` parsed as an ordinary throw.
- check_arrow(): a new gate replacing every `check(TokenType.ARROW)`
  arrow-detection site, so `x \n => x` no longer reads as an arrow function
  (§15.3). The hoisting/param scanners keep the plain token check: they only
  skip over an arrow body and never decide acceptance.
- last_was_newline_yield: a bare `yield` ended by a line terminator is a
  complete YieldExpression, so binary_expr stops rather than taking it as a
  left operand (§15.5). It breaks out instead of erroring, which leaves the
  statement level to apply ASI — `yield \n + 1` stays legal as a fresh
  `+1` ExpressionStatement while `yield \n * 1` fails, `*` being unable to
  start a statement.

commits.subject: fix(vm): report a non-iterable for-of/destructuring source as not iterable
commits.body:
`for (var x of ([1],[2])[0]) {}` threw "TypeError: undefined is not a
function". The type was right and control flow was correct, but the message
described the engine's internal iterator-protocol lookup instead of the
user's mistake, and implied something had been called.

Unlike spread and yield*, which run a real GetIterator in the VM, for-of and
array destructuring compiled the protocol to a bare GETPROP of
src[@@iterator] followed by CALL, so a missing method surfaced as the generic
call error. A new CHKITER opcode runs the GetIterator validation the two
paths were missing, emitted by both compiler sites (the shared
emit_iter_open and emit_destruct_iter_setup) so the rule has one home:

  C=1, before the @@iterator read: a null/undefined source is not iterable.
       Previously the read itself failed, producing "Cannot read properties
       of null" with the internal key rendered as raw bytes.
  C=0, after the read: a missing method means "X is not iterable"; a present
       but non-callable one keeps the distinct "X is not a function", the
       same distinction node draws. These are different mistakes.
  C=2, after the call: GetIterator step 5 requires an Object. This check did
       not exist for for-of/destructuring at all -- a spec gap, not just a
       message issue -- so `{[Symbol.iterator](){return 42}}` failed later on
       the .next read.

Two adjacent fixes fell out of the differential:

- for-await over a primitive was broken, not merely misreported.
  to_object_for_method returned null for any non-object on the assumption
  that "for-await sources are always objects in practice", so @@iterator on
  the wrapper prototype was unreachable and `for await (c of "ab")` threw
  instead of iterating. It now boxes via the existing to_object_for_lookup.
- GET_ITER_ASYNC's two "is not async iterable" throws had an empty subject,
  printing " is not async iterable" with no value named.

Spread's "Cannot spread null" and yield*'s "GetIterator: result is not an
object" are reworded to match, so one mistake reads the same in every form,
and null is named "null" rather than typeof's "object".

Message text is deliberately not matched to node byte-for-byte: node
reconstructs the source expression ("([1] , [2])[0]", "{(intermediate
value)}") via V8's CallPrinter, and its wording differs between its own
forms for the same input. test262 asserts only the error type. The new test
asserts the type everywhere plus the iterable/not-a-function distinction,
and passes unmodified under node.

commits.subject: fix(json): serialize a typed array's integer-indexed own keys
commits.body:
JSON.stringify(new Int32Array([1,2,3])) returned "{}" instead of
{"0":1,"1":2,"2":3}. SerializeJSONObject uses EnumerableOwnPropertyNames,
and for an integer-indexed exotic the own keys are the canonical numeric
indices served by the exotic handler. json_serialize_object had its own
key walk over obj.prop_count, which only sees the named property table, so
those indices were invisible to it.

The same blindness appeared twice in the one function: the `has_props`
early-out also tested prop_count alone, short-circuiting a bare typed array
to "{}" before the key loop could run. Fixing only the walk still returned
"{}" for a typed array with no named properties.

Rather than adding a third bespoke exotic branch (for-in already carries one
in collect_forin_keys), both sites now use the shared collector in object.c3
that Object.keys/entries/values already use, which knows every own-key
source. It produces exactly the order the bespoke code hand-rolled --
integer indices ascending, then String keys in insertion order, Symbols and
non-enumerables excluded -- so ~60 lines of duplicated sorting and
concatenation go away. collect_own_enum_string_keys now takes a Heap*
instead of a BuiltinContext*, since heap was the only field it used and JSON
has no BuiltinContext.

DataView and ArrayBuffer are not integer-indexed exotics and still serialize
as "{}". Verified against node across 11 typed-array kinds x {empty, len 1,
len 1000, detached, extra named props, toJSON, nested in object/array,
replacer function, replacer array, space, round-trip}: 162/162 rows
identical, including BigInt-backed arrays throwing TypeError in both.

commits.subject: Merge for-head var binding fixes (three root causes)
commits.body:
function f(){ for (var v in {z:1}) {} return v; } returned undefined
where node gives 'z'. Global scope was unaffected, and for-of had the
same defect.

Three causes, not one, and the first is the reverse of what I guessed:

1. The head called declare_var, which ALWAYS allocates, so it wrote a
   fresh register while reads used the hoisted one — then the loop
   epilogue's pop_scope_to dropped the head's entry. New
   declare_binding_var reuses the hoisted register for a VAR kind;
   let/const still declare fresh. Global scope was immune because the
   head's DECLVAR keeps the env slot correct and global reads go
   through GETVAR — the same immunity explains why arrow and closure
   contexts already worked.

2. A re-run of the 7ffb9b4a class: the DECLARING for-in head still
   pointed NEXTFOR straight at the binding register, so the exhausting
   step clobbered it with undefined. NEXTFOR now writes a scratch
   register and the copy happens after the exhaustion branch.

3. hoist_decls bailed at the first non-IDENTIFIER declarator, so
   var [a] and var {p:b} hoisted nothing — which also broke plain
   pattern var statements in nested blocks:
   function f(){ { var [z] = [3]; } return z; } threw.

commits.subject: Merge AssignmentTargetType split from the register-aliasing hint
commits.body:
(x = y) = 1 and (x ??= y)++ were accepted. The obvious fix — clearing
last_was_local_var to reject them — would have been a MISCOMPILE, not
just a different bug: that flag doubles as the register-aliasing hint
that fires binary_expr's copy-to-temp guard, so clearing it turns a
missing SyntaxError into a wrong value. b0fdc49c set the flag precisely
to make (u = 45) > 0 compile correctly.

Two agents previously declined this task and I broke the engine myself
in adjacent code, so the gating was the point: assignment_expr now
stamps a SEPARATE last_target_invalid verdict on exit, leaving the
aliasing hint untouched. Emitted bytecode for fib, k, t = t + 1 and
(u = 45) > 0 is BYTE-IDENTICAL to main — the strongest available proof
the allocator contract is unchanged. Goldens 28/28, never regenerated.
fib(10) = 55, k(7) = 7.

The ordering trap worth recording: the verdict cannot be set where the
assignment operator is consumed. Parsing the RHS resolves an identifier,
and identifiers legitimately CLEAR the verdict since they are valid
targets — so x = y set it and had y immediately wipe it. The first build
was green on goldens and shapes while the differential was completely
unchanged at 97 mismatches. Hence the wrapper.

Scope was larger than filed: not 4 or 8 forms but 97 mismatching source
shapes, collapsing onto 10 newly-passing test262 tests. Phase 2 12 -> 2
fail; all other phases unchanged; the four apparent losses are the known
S7.8.5_A*_T2 regexp timeouts, each re-verified PASS standalone.

Local 289 scripts, both RSS guards at 100%.

Pre-existing and deliberately not touched: node accepts (f()) = 1 and

commits.subject: fix(compiler): an assignment's result is not a SimpleAssignmentTarget
commits.body:
`(x = y) = 1` and `(x ??= y)++` were silently accepted. Per ES §13.15.1 an
AssignmentExpression has AssignmentTargetType ~invalid~, so both are early
SyntaxErrors.

The reason this was left standing is that last_was_local_var answers two
different questions with one bit:

  1. "is this a valid SimpleAssignmentTarget?"  — read by the four target
     checks in assignment_expr / unary_expr INC,DEC / postfix_expr
  2. "does the result live in a local's home register, so an enclosing
     operator must copy it to a temp before using it as a destination?" —
     the aliasing hint b0fdc49c added so `(u = 45) > 0` stops clobbering u

An assignment result needs (2) but must not get (1). Clearing the shared
flag — the obvious fix — silently disables the copy-to-temp guard and
corrupts the target variable's register, which is a wrong-value bug, not a
parse error. So the verdict gets its own field, last_target_invalid, read
only by the four target checks and by no codegen path at all. The reference
markers and every allocator decision are untouched, and the emitted
bytecode for the fusion/recursion shapes is byte-identical (verified by
disassembly diff and by 28/28 unregenerated goldens).

Setting the verdict has to happen after the inner parse returns, not where
the operator is consumed: parsing the RHS resolves identifiers, and every
resolved identifier retires the verdict (an IdentifierReference IS a valid
target), so `x = y` would set it and have `y` immediately wipe it. Hence
the thin assignment_expr wrapper over assignment_expr_inner.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): a pattern default must not swallow the pattern's closing bracket
commits.body:
hoist_var_pattern skipped a default value (`= expr`) with skip_expression,
which stops on ',' and ';' but CONSUMES a ']' or '}' at its own top level —
that bracket is the enclosing pattern's closer. The walk therefore lost the end
of the pattern and ran on into the initializer, hoisting names out of it:

    var { w: [x] = [4] } = { w: [7] };   // bound `w`, which is a KEY

skip_pattern_default stops at a ',', ']', '}' or ')' seen at nesting depth 0
and pushes it back, so the walk sees the pattern's own structure.

values but assert the key's unboundness through a closure, where the binding is

commits.subject: fix(compiler): a `var` for-head writes the hoisted binding, and patterns hoist
commits.body:
Three defects made a `var` for-in/for-of head lose its binding at FUNCTION
scope while working at global scope. All were silent wrong answers in
completely ordinary code.

1. The head called declare_var unconditionally, which always allocates. A
   `var` name is already hoisted to the enclosing function scope, so the head
   wrote into a FRESH register while reads outside the loop used the hoisted
   one; the head's own scope entry was then dropped at the loop epilogue's
   pop_scope_to. New declare_binding_var reuses the hoisted register for VAR
   and declares fresh for let/const, mirroring the plain `for (var i = ...)`
   and identifier `var` statement sites. Applied at the four for-head sites
   and the two destructuring-declarator sites, which had the same shape.

     function f(){ for (var v in {z:1}) {} return v; }   undefined, not 'z'

2. The for-in head pointed NEXTFOR straight at the binding register. The
   exhausting step reports has_next=false and writes undefined to its A
   operand, clobbering the binding on the way out even after (1). NEXTFOR now
   targets a scratch and the key moves into the binding past the exhaustion
   branch — the shape emit_bare_forin_loop already used.

3. hoist_decls' declarator loop stopped at the first non-IDENTIFIER token, so
   a binding PATTERN (`var [a]`, `var {p: b}`) hoisted nothing at all. For a
   plain statement that was masked because var_declaration declares as it
   parses; a for-head is not, so `for (var [x] of []) {} x` threw
   "x is not defined". hoist_var_pattern token-walks the pattern and hoists
   each leaf BoundName, skipping default values and computed keys (whose
   identifiers are references, not bindings). This also fixes plain pattern
   `var` statements in nested/unexecuted blocks, which were equally unhoisted.

Both bugs are invisible at global scope and for captured locals — both are
env-resident, so the head's DECLVAR keeps the env slot correct and reads go
through GETVAR. Only register-resident function locals diverge, which is why
the regression coverage reads every binding from inside a function without
closing over it.

member, computed, array/object destructuring, bare destructuring} x {global,
function, nested function, method, arrow, generator, closure} x {0, 1, many
iterations}: 392/462 matching before, 456/462 after, none newly broken. The 6
remaining are a separate pre-existing bug (compile_arrow_inner never calls
hoist_decls, so arrow bodies hoist no `var` at all), verified present at
6c492b9c and untouched here.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): the for-of head's RHS is an AssignmentExpression
commits.body:

after `of`, not an Expression, so a top-level comma there terminates nothing
and is a SyntaxError. All six for-of RHS positions were calling the full
comma-expression parser, which silently swallowed the comma and ran the loop
over the LAST operand: `for (let x of [], [2])` iterated [2].

The contrast is what makes this specific to for-of. A for-in RHS *is* a full
Expression, and the C-style for's clauses are Expressions too, so the comma
stays legal in both -- those heads are untouched, and the test asserts it.

commits.subject: fix(module): an ImportedBinding is a BindingIdentifier

names (`eval`, `arguments`, `let`, `yield`, ...) are illegal there. Two of the
four ImportedBinding positions read the name with a bare `expect(IDENTIFIER)`
and accepted them:

  - the ImportSpecifier alias, `import { x as eval } from "./m.mjs"`

`import { x as let }` paths already used -- that split is why the rule held in
some import forms but not others.

The bare `import { eval }` form needs its own check rather than the helper: its
single name is simultaneously the ModuleExportName and the binding, and it is
parsed by parse_module_export_name, which deliberately also admits string
literals and keywords because an export NAME may be anything. Only the binding
half is restricted, so `import { "x" as z }` and `import { a as evaluate }`
keep working.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): new.target is a SyntaxError in top-level code
commits.body:
ES2024 §16.1.1 (Script) and §16.2.1.1 (Module): it is a Syntax Error for a
StatementList to Contain NewTarget "unless the source code containing
NewTarget is eval code that is being processed by a direct eval that is
contained in function code that is not the function code of an ArrowFunction."

Only the eval half of that sentence was implemented. The surrounding comment
already claimed "top-level code is already rejected by is_global +
!constructable", but no such test existed, so `new.target;` at the top level of
a script or module compiled to a NEWTARGET opcode.

An ArrowFunction written directly in top-level code is covered by the same
rule: it has no [[NewTarget]] of its own and inherits from an enclosing
function that does not exist. That needs a dedicated flag rather than
propagating is_global into the arrow context -- is_global also governs where
declarations are registered, and carrying it in made the arrow body's own

commits.subject: fix(module): enforce duplicate ExportedNames and module LexicallyDeclaredNames
commits.body:
Two module early errors were unenforced:

  §16.2.3.1  the ExportedNames of a ModuleItemList must contain no duplicates
  §16.2.1.1  a module body's LexicallyDeclaredNames must contain no duplicates

For the first, every named export already funnels through
mod_register_export, so the check goes in a thin CompilerContext wrapper at
that one point and all eleven call sites route through it. That covers every
spelling that can collide -- `export {x}` twice, two `as` aliases onto one
name, `export default` paired with `{y as default}`, two same-named
`export function` declarations, and `export * as z` against a local
`{x as z}`. `export * from` stays exempt: it contributes no ExportedName of
its own, which is why it registers through mod_register_star_export and never
reaches this path.

The second is a rule Scripts do not have. A module's top-level
FunctionDeclarations are lexical, so `class F {} function F(){}` is an error
here while the same pair is legal at Script top level, where the function is
var-scoped and simply wins. The check reuses the name sets the module prologue
already builds -- the let/const/class spans from pre_scan_lexical_decls and the
function names hoist_global_fn_decls records -- so it adds no new scan.
`export default function F(){}` needs its own check at the binding site: its
name is not in statement position, so the hoisting pre-scan never records it.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): enforce lexical-vs-parameter and duplicate-BoundName early errors
commits.body:
Three related early errors were unenforced, all of them cases where a lexical
binding may not collide with a parameter or with itself:

  §14.1.2   a function body's top-level LexicallyDeclaredNames must not
            contain any BoundName of the parameter list
  §14.15.1  the same for a catch block and its CatchParameter, including when
            the lexical declaration is a block-level FunctionDeclaration or a
            class (both lexical in strict code), plus the requirement that a
            destructuring CatchParameter's BoundNames be unique
  §14.7.5.1 a `let`/`const` ForDeclaration's BoundNames must be unique

What made this need more than a name comparison is that a body `var` of the
same name stays legal in every one of these positions -- it denotes the very
same binding -- so `kind` alone cannot distinguish the cases. Parameters are
pushed onto scope_stack as VAR (they share var's register and env treatment),
so ScopeEntry gains an `is_param` flag, and the collision check keys off that
rather than the kind.

The scope boundary needed the same care. A nested block's lexical names shadow
the parameters freely, so the walk stops at a block marker -- but the marker
the function body itself pushes has to be transparent, or the parameters just
below it are never reached. ScopeEntry.is_body_mark records which markers are
body scopes (function bodies, and catch blocks, whose relationship to their
CatchParameter is the same one). The walk crosses at most one: crossing a
second would reach an enclosing function's parameters, which the declaration is
free to shadow.

Duplicate BoundNames reuse SeenParams, which already implements exactly that
check for FormalParameters, rather than growing a second duplicate-name walk.
A `var` for-head stays exempt, since `for (var [x, x] of ...)` names one
binding twice and is legal.

commits.subject: Merge cyclic-array guard and growable JSON buffers
commits.body:
Two value-serialization bugs, both bigger than filed.

Cyclic arrays SIGSEGV'd: Array.prototype.join recursed on a
self-reference with no cycle guard, reachable from ordinary code with
no console involved. A heap-level join_visited set now bails out,
matching node's semantics where a cycle contributes an empty string.

toLocaleString needed a native rewrite rather than a guard: it was
compiled JS whose environment is the global object, so it could not
reach an internal guard without exposing one to user code. Node shares
the in-progress set between join and toLocaleString — a cycle through
either bails — so one heap-level set is correct only if both are
native. It re-satisfies all 12 test262 toLocaleString tests.

JSON was FIVE caps, not the one output buffer I filed. The headline
symptom — a 2000-key object stringifying to 557 chars — came from a
64-KEY PROPERTY SNAPSHOT, so fixing only the buffer would have left it
intact. Also a 4096-byte escape buffer clipping strings at 4095,
1024-byte key buffers, and a 1024-byte buffer in JSON.PARSE that
rejected longer string literals as SyntaxError. The round trip was
broken from both ends: the engine emitted documents it could not read
back. All five now grow, and over-large output throws
RangeError: Invalid string length, matching node's type and message.

Verified against node: 16/16 cyclic cases and 9/9 siblings (Proxy,
typed array, array-like, diamond, unwind-after-cycle) byte-identical;
the JSON differential's only remaining rows are two pre-existing
typed-array cases identical on both sides. Regression files are 26 and
52 checks, engine == node, and on baseline give exit 139 and a parser
error respectively.

test262 phases 0-8, 11: zero regressions, comm-diffed. Local 284
scripts, golden 28/28, both RSS guards green.

Deliberately NOT matched: node renders a cyclic array as
<ref *1> [ [Circular *1] ] via util.inspect, while this engine renders
via toString(). Matching that means implementing util.inspect wholesale.
The crash is gone and output matches node's String() semantics.

commits.subject: fix(json): grow the serializer buffer instead of truncating
commits.body:
JSON.stringify returned SUCCESS carrying malformed, unterminated JSON once a
value outgrew a fixed buffer -- no error, no exception, no marker. A 2000-key
object stringified to 557 characters where node produces 23781. A correct
looking return value carrying corrupt data is the worst failure shape for an
API that things round-trip through.

Four separate caps, all silent:
  - a 16384-byte output buffer,
  - a 4096-byte per-string escape buffer (strings clipped at 4095 chars),
  - 1024-byte per-key escape buffers,
  - a 64-entry property-key snapshot (objects clipped at 64 keys).
A fifth, in JSON.parse, rejected any string literal over 1024 bytes as a
SyntaxError, so a document this engine emitted would not parse back -- the
round trip failed from both ends.

All five now grow to fit, through a shared StrBuf that reports allocation
failure rather than clipping. The only remaining limit is memory, and hitting
it throws RangeError: Invalid string length, which is what node throws at its
own limits.

The console %j specifier inherited the 16384-byte cap by construction; it
follows the same path now and renders a 2000-key object in full.

escape-heavy and long strings, unicode and surrogate pairs, BigInt, Infinity/
NaN, Date, Map/Set, replacer function, replacer array and the space argument:
byte-identical output, with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) stable for every
case.

commits.subject: fix(array): guard Array.prototype.join against cyclic arrays
commits.body:
`var a = []; a.push(a); String(a)` crashed with SIGSEGV. A self-referencing
element converts through Array.prototype.toString, which calls join again on
the same array, so join recursed until the C stack was exhausted. Reachable
from ordinary user code -- String(), a template literal, and console.log with
a plain array argument all route into join.

Track the arrays currently being joined on the heap rather than in one
invocation's frame: a cycle re-enters join through a separate call, so a
per-call set cannot see it. An array already on the set contributes the empty
string to the level that re-enters it, matching V8.

Array.prototype.toLocaleString shared the defect and, in node, shares the
in-progress set with join -- a cycle through either bails out. It was compiled
JS whose environment is the global object, so it could not reach an internal
guard without exposing one to user code; reimplemented natively against the
spec loop so it uses the same set. Its output is now assembled in a growable
StrBuf instead of an intermediate elements array.

frozen/Proxy/array-like cycle shapes times String, join, join(sep), toString,
toLocaleString, template literal and console.log: byte-identical, and the set

commits.subject: Merge for-in/for-of member-head codegen state cleanup
commits.body:
A member-target for-in left three pieces of state behind from its
discarded head parse. One is load-bearing: call_prop_obj_reg stayed
set, so the next call took the method-call path with undef_this false,
and neither the CALL_VAR fusion nor the GETVAR-restore branch ran —
both are gated on it. The callee's read had already been stripped, so
CALL dispatched on a never-written register.

Separately, the speculative code from the discarded parse was never
rewound, emitting LDCONST over a live local's home register — silent
corruption of unrelated locals, no crash required.

irrelevant; the trigger is a CALL AFTER a member-target loop in a
non-global function. A lone loop followed by print() crashes, and two
member loops with no following call do not. The original repro only
implicated a preceding loop because its print came last.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): clear method-call receiver state after a for-in/of member head
commits.body:
A for-in/of head whose LHS is a member expression (`for (o.p in x)`) is
parsed twice speculatively and then discarded: the real store is re-parsed
from a lexer snapshot once per iteration. Both discarded parses restored the
lexer but left compiler state behind that later expressions read as if it
described the most recently emitted instruction.

The load-bearing leak is call_prop_obj_reg, which records a method call's
receiver. Left set by the discarded head, the next call anywhere in the same
function took the method-call path, so `undef_this` was false and neither the
CALL_VAR fusion nor the GETVAR/GETGLOBAL restore branch ran -- both are
gated on it. The callee's read had already been stripped from the code
stream speculatively, so the call dispatched on a register nothing ever
wrote: "string is not a function" / "object is not a function".

Two further leaks are fixed alongside it:

  * The speculative parse's emitted GETPROP/GETPROPC were never rewound, so
    the head's LHS executed once before the loop. Its scratch registers are
    allocated from next_reg, which still overlaps the enclosing function's
    locals, so this silently clobbered a live local (`LDCONST r1, 1` over
    `o`'s home register). Rewind code_count, matching the existing idiom in
    destructuring.c3.
  * last_was_getvar/last_was_getglobal anchor the CALL_VAR fusion to
    `last_getvar_code_pos + 1 == code_count`; after a rewind that equality
    can hold for an unrelated instruction.

The blast radius was the whole enclosing function rather than the loop, and
the register clobber corrupted unrelated locals with no diagnostic.

Note the trigger is a call *after* the loop, not a preceding loop as first
suspected: a lone member-target loop followed by any call crashes, and two
member loops with no following call do not.

test/forin_forof_assignment_target.js drops the workaround that isolated each
member-target case in its own function. New test/forin_forof_member_head.js
covers {for-in, for-of} x {o.p, a[i], o.a.b} x {no preceding loop, bare-id,
declaring, member, destructuring} x {global, function, nested, method} plus
the error paths; 52 assertions, identical counts under node.

commits.body:

argument space-separated, so "a %s b" with "X" printed "a %s b X" instead of
"a X b".

Adds a single formatter shared by every console method that takes a format
string — log/info/debug/trace/warn/error and assert's message arguments —
rather than a copy per method. It replaces the two near-identical
stdout/stderr loops with one implementation parameterised by a byte sink.

Reference is node's util.format, not the bare WHATWG Formatter, since real
code is written against node; the header comment records where the two
disagree (%j, %o detail, %c) and why. Substitution is gated on the first
argument being a string AND at least one further argument existing, which is
also why "pct %% end" alone keeps both percent signs while "pct %% end" with
an argument collapses them — the gate is argument count, not console-vs-util.

Semantics verified against node v24 rather than assumed:
  - %d/%i/%f are three different coercions (Number / parseInt / parseFloat),
    so a boolean is 1 under %d but NaN under %i, and [1,2] is NaN under %d
    but 1 under %i via the string form. %i/%f delegate to the real
    parseInt/parseFloat instead of reimplementing the prefix grammar.
  - %s on a Symbol prints Symbol(desc); ToString would throw, and the raw
    HString carries marker bytes that must not reach the output.
  - %j maps a cycle to [Circular] rather than the TypeError JSON.stringify
    raises, and reports undefined/functions/symbols as undefined at the root.

falls through to the trailing append and Array.prototype.toString recurses.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): preserve AssignmentTargetType through parens and delete
commits.body:
Three related AssignmentTargetType defects (ES2024 §13.15.1).

Parentheses PRESERVE AssignmentTargetType, so `(eval) = 1`, `(eval)++`
and `(arguments) += 1` are still the forbidden strict-mode assignments.
They do NOT preserve IsIdentifierRef, so `(fn) = function(){}` must
leave the function anonymous (§13.15.2 step 1.c). One field was serving
both rules, and clearing it at every `)` for the second silently
disabled the first. The parenthesized-ness is now tracked separately,
and the name is kept only when the group really was an identifier
reference — otherwise it is a leftover from an inner operand.

`delete` yields a boolean, never a Reference, so like every other
UnaryExpression (§13.5) its target type is ~invalid~ and
`delete x.y = 1` is a SyntaxError. The delete path cleared only the
member marker, leaving the operand's identifier markers to masquerade as
a valid target.

Third, found by the must-still-accept half of the test rather than by
any failing test262 case: an assignment that supplies no inferred name
did not clear one left by an earlier assignment, so
`(w = 2) * (w = 3); (fn) = function(){}` named the function "w". That
predates this branch; the fix is the else-branch on the NamedEvaluation
capture.

NOT fixed, and left for a follow-up: `(x = y) = 1` and `(x = y)++` are
still accepted. An assignment's own result is ~invalid~ as a target, but
last_was_local_var is deliberately re-set on the way out of
assignment_expr as a register-aliasing hint ("`left` IS the target's
home register, copy it before reusing"), which is what makes
`(u = 45) > 0` compile correctly. Target-validity and register-aliasing
share that one flag, so separating them is a real change to the register
allocator's contract rather than a local fix. 4 of the 12
assignmenttargettype failures remain for that reason.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): enforce `**` and `??` operand restrictions
commits.body:
Two cases where the spec uses a distinct production rather than another
precedence level, so a precedence table alone cannot express them.

`ExponentiationExpression : UpdateExpression ** ExponentiationExpression`
(§13.6): the LEFT operand is an UpdateExpression, so `-a ** b` is a
SyntaxError — the grammar refuses to guess between `(-a) ** b` and
`-(a ** b)`. unary_expr now reports whether it consumed a unary operator
and binary_expr rejects that as a `**` left operand. The flag is applied
after the recursive operand parse (hence the unary_expr/unary_expr_inner
split): every operator case recurses for its operand, and the inner call
would otherwise overwrite the field with the operand's shape. `a ** -b`,
`++a ** b`, `a++ ** b` and `1 - 2 ** 2` all stay legal.

`CoalesceExpression : CoalesceExpressionHead ?? BitwiseORExpression`
(§13.13): `??` cannot be mixed with an unparenthesized `&&` / `||` in
either order. `??` sits directly below `||` in the precedence table, so
the mix parsed silently. Two things fix it: the `??` right operand is now
parsed at PREC_BITWISE_OR (matching the production) instead of prec + 1,
which leaves a following `||` unconsumed, and one binary_expr invocation
now refuses to see both operator families. Parenthesised forms are parsed
by a nested invocation with its own flags, so `(a && b) ?? c` and
`a ?? (b || c)` stay legal, as does `a ?? b | c`.

Runtime semantics are unchanged and were diffed against node, including
`**` right-associativity (2 ** 3 ** 2 === 512) and `null ?? 1 | 2 === 3`.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject `async function` as a single-statement body
commits.body:
An AsyncFunctionDeclaration / AsyncGeneratorDeclaration is a
Declaration, so it is not a Statement and cannot be an if/else arm, a
loop body or a labelled statement — those positions admit `Statement`,
not `StatementListItem` (§14.4-§14.7, §14.13). statement_body() already
rejected `function`, `function*`, `class`, `let` and `const` by
switching on the body's leading token, but `async` is a contextual
keyword that lexes as a plain IDENTIFIER, so the async forms were
silently accepted.

The check cannot be a lookahead in statement_body(): consuming and
pushing back the `async` token there desynchronises `lexer.token_start`,
which statement() refreshes precisely to fix the
Function.prototype.toString span of this declaration form, and doing so
broke the parse of the builtin prelude. Instead statement_body() sets a
one-shot flag that statement() consumes at the exact point it has
already classified `async` + `function` on the same line, so there is
one lookahead rather than two.

`async` remains an ordinary identifier everywhere else, and §14.7's
[no LineTerminator here] still splits `if (1) async\nfunction f(){}`
into two statements; both are covered by the accept half of the test.

commits.subject: docs(compiler): cite the grammar for `new import()` rejection
commits.body:
Records why `new import('').then` stays a SyntaxError here even though
V8/node accept it. `MemberExpression` lists PrimaryExpression, indexing,
`. IdentifierName`, TemplateLiteral, SuperProperty, MetaProperty,
`new MemberExpression Arguments` and `. PrivateIdentifier`; ImportCall
appears only under CallExpression, and there is no
`MemberExpression : CallExpression` production. Both `new` productions
(`MemberExpression : new MemberExpression Arguments` and
`NewExpression : new NewExpression`) bottom out at MemberExpression, so
no `new` callee can contain a bare ImportCall — including one with a
property access chained onto it, since `CallExpression . IdentifierName`
is still a CallExpression.

MetaProperty IS a MemberExpression production, so `new import.meta` and
`new import.meta.foo` correctly parse and fail at runtime with a "not a
constructor" TypeError rather than being rejected early.

test262 has no case either way. QuickJS matches this reading exactly on
both counts, so node is the outlier and its leniency is not copied.
Behaviour is unchanged; this commit is the citation.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): switch CaseBlock early errors; drop sloppy-only Annex B relaxation
commits.body:
A switch's CaseBlock is a single StatementList spanning every clause
(§14.12.1), so it gets the same two duplicate-name early errors a
BlockStatement does: no duplicate LexicallyDeclaredNames, and no name in
both LexicallyDeclaredNames and VarDeclaredNames. The CaseBlock scope
and its pre-scan already existed — `let f; ... let f;` was caught by the
declaration-site check — but neither early error ran over the pre-scan
result, so the cross-kind cases (`let f; ... class f {}`) and the
lexical/var cases (`var f; ... let f`) were accepted. Both checks are
factored out of block() and called from both sites, so the two scopes
cannot diverge again. The stale "delegated to a separate call site"
comment on the var check described a call site that did not exist.

Also drops `redeclarable_fn`. It suppressed the duplicate error for a
pair of plain FunctionDeclarations per Annex B, but that relaxation is
sloppy-mode only and this engine is strict-only. test262 states the
split directly: the generated tests for `{ function f(){} function f(){} }`
and its switch counterpart come from the `redeclare-allow-sloppy-function`
templates and carry `flags: [onlyStrict]` with `negative: phase: parse`.
A function BODY is unaffected — its top-level function declarations are
var-scoped, not lexical, so they never reach this check.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): accept `await` as a LabelIdentifier in script code
commits.body:
`await: ;` is a valid labelled statement outside a module and outside an
async function/arrow: a LabelIdentifier is an Identifier (§14.13), and
§13.1.1 makes `await` an ordinary IdentifierName wherever it is not
reserved. The engine already applied that rule for binding identifiers
(`var await = 1;`) but its label branch keyed on the IDENTIFIER token
type alone, and `await` lexes as its own AWAIT token, so a legal label
was refused. This was an over-rejection: it broke working script code.

Both sides of a label now share one predicate, so the definition
(`await: ;`) and the reference (`break await;` / `continue await;`)
cannot drift apart. `yield` deliberately gets no such relaxation —
§13.1.1 reserves it in all strict-mode code and this engine is
strict-only — and `await` stays reserved in a module, in an async
function/arrow, and at a class static block's top level.

commits.subject: Merge for-in/for-of head assignment semantics
commits.body:
Two defects, the second worse than the one filed.

1. An undeclared bare target was accepted, creating an implicit global.
   The head bypasses the assignment path 352b1471 fixed. Affected both
   for-in and for-of.

2. UNREPORTED AND WORSE: for-in never assigned its target at all.
   var y; for (y in {a:1,b:2}) {} left y === undefined — the store sat
   before the exhaustion branch, so the final NEXTFOR (has_next=false,
   iter_var=undefined) overwrote the binding on the way out. Silent
   wrong answer in a completely ordinary construct; 31k test262 tests
   never caught it. for-of was unaffected.

Fixing (2) is what makes (1) correct: node accepts
for (x in {}) {} for undeclared x because the assignment never runs, so
changing the opcode without moving the store would have thrown
spuriously on an empty iterable. Error type is a runtime ReferenceError,
not a parse-time SyntaxError — confirmed against node, which throws only
when an iteration actually occurs.

emit_bare_forin_loop moves the store after the IF_FALSE exhaustion
branch, switches PUTVAR to PUTVAR_ASSIGN, and gains the
register-resident-local fast path bare for-of already had.
emit_head_bind's env-resident bare branch gets the same opcode change.

Found by building the ACCEPT table first, as the previous early-error
work established: the reject-side probes all looked fine, and defect (2)
was only visible from the accept side.

MD5-identical; the comm pipeline was control-tested by removing 3 lines
and confirming it reported exactly 3. Local 277 scripts, golden 28/28,
both RSS guards green.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): for-in/for-of heads are assignment positions
commits.body:
The bare-identifier target of a for-in/for-of head was published with
PUTVAR, an *initialization* store. Two bugs followed.

1. Strict-only violation. PUTVAR falls back to env_put(var_env) when the
   name resolves nowhere, creating an implicit global, so
   `for (x in {a:1}) {}` with x never declared was accepted. Node throws
   ReferenceError. This is the for-in/for-of sibling of the implicit-
   globals hole closed in 352b1471; the head simply never routed through
   the assignment path that emits PUTVAR_ASSIGN.

   Both bare paths now emit PUTVAR_ASSIGN, which throws
   "'x' is not defined" for an unresolved target and additionally gives
   const/TDZ targets the same throw any other assignment gets.

2. for-in never assigned its target at all. The store was emitted BEFORE
   the IF_FALSE exhaustion test, so the final NEXTFOR (has_next=false,
   iter_var=undefined) overwrote the binding with undefined on the way
   out: `var y; for (y in {a:1}) {}` left y === undefined instead of "a".
   Silent, and the suite never caught it. The store now follows the
   branch, which is also what makes the empty-iterable case legal --
   node accepts `for (x in {}) {}` for undeclared x because the
   assignment never executes.

   A register-cached local target is written straight into its home
   register (LDREG) rather than via the env, mirroring the fix the bare
   for-of path already carried in emit_head_bind: PUTVAR updates only the
   env slot and then clears its source, desyncing the body's register
   read.

Verified against node over {for-in, for-of} x {undeclared bare, declared
var/let/const, member, computed member, array/object/nested destructuring,
defaults, rest}: reject table 11/11 and accept table 39/39 agree. The one
residual difference is TypeError message wording on a nested destructuring
pattern, which is pre-existing and type-identical.

commits.subject: Merge finally-completion fixes for non-escaping break/continue
commits.body:
Two silent wrong answers, both sync and neither generator-specific.

The compiler emitted BREAK/CONTINUE — the 'may cross a finally' forms
that make the VM park the completion on the innermost catcher and divert
— for EVERY break and continue, including ones that never leave the
try/catch/finally region. When they don't, the IN_FINALLY guard at
vm_control.c3:746 pops and FREES the catcher to avoid looping, throwing
away the completion parked on it. Confirmed against node:

  try { throw E } finally { while(1) break; }
      swallowed the exception entirely, rc=0, no output
  for(i..){ try{ switch(i){case 0: break;} ... } finally{ ... } }
      ran the finally twice and out of order

push_loop now records try_depth, and loop_jump_op emits a plain JUMP
when the target loop lives at or inside the current depth.
patch_continue_chain preserves each site's opcode instead of hardcoding
CONTINUE.

Second, independent root cause fixed in the same commit: a for-of body
opens its own IteratorClose-on-throw TRY around bind+body, and jumping
out bypassed its ENDTRY, leaving a stale catcher on act.cat. A later
ENDFINALLY then popped the stale for-of catcher instead of its own, so
  try { throw E } finally { for (v of it) break; }
also produced no output and rc=0. emit_unwind_iter_close now emits
ENDTRY; it only pops finally-less catchers, so it cannot eat a finally's.

43-case differential (yield-in-finally, yield* delegation,
return-through-finally, async generators, await-in-finally, 18
break/continue-across-try variants, and the sync equivalents of each):
4 mismatched before, 43/43 match node after.

after, 0 regressions, FAIL sets byte-identical. Local 276 scripts;
forin-rss and generator-catcher-rss green.

One golden regenerated: loop_backedge_labeled's CONTINUE +5 becomes
JUMP +5. Its source contains no try at all, so a labeled continue that
could never cross a finally now compiles to a plain jump; its
behavioural pair still passes.

NOTE the original repro filed for this bug already passed on baseline —
the reported mechanism (a generator resume failing to restore the parked
completion) was wrong, and gs.cat's deliberate suspend-time aliasing was
not touched.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): don't route a non-escaping break/continue through the finally
commits.body:
BREAK/CONTINUE are the "may cross a finally" jump forms: the VM parks the
target on the innermost catcher and diverts to its finally block. The
compiler emitted them for every break/continue regardless of whether the
jump actually left the try/catch/finally region it was written in. When it
did not, the VM's IN_FINALLY guard popped and FREED the catcher to avoid
looping, discarding the completion parked on it.

Three silent wrong answers fall out of that, all reproduced against node:

  try { throw e } finally { while (1) break; }     e vanished, rc=0
  for (i..) { try { switch(i){case 0: break;} } finally { log('f') } }
                                                  ran the finally twice
  try { for(i..){ for(j..){ break; } } throw e } catch(e){}
                                                  Uncaught: e

The last one has no finally in the inner loop at all -- a plain nested-loop
break inside a try turned a caught exception into a fatal uncaught one.

LoopInfo now records try_depth at loop entry and loop_jump_op picks a plain
JUMP when the target loop lives at or inside the current try_depth, so no
boundary is crossed. patch_continue_chain preserves each site's opcode
instead of hardcoding CONTINUE.

A for-of body opens its own IteratorClose-on-throw TRY around bind+body; a
jump out of the body bypassed that TRY's ENDTRY and left the guard catcher
on act.cat. Usually absorbed harmlessly, but an ENDFINALLY reached
afterwards then popped the stale for-of catcher instead of its own, so
`try { throw e } finally { for (v of it) break; }` lost e entirely (rc=0,
no output). emit_unwind_iter_close now emits the ENDTRY alongside the
ITER_CLOSE it already emitted at every abrupt-exit site.

The reported generator symptom (a parked exception lost across a yield in a
finally) is the same defect: its finally contained a loop break. The plain
non-loop generator forms already passed after 4775fec4; gs.cat aliasing and
chains_restore_from_gen are untouched.

commits.subject: Merge four early-error families: yield, escaped keywords, module positions, new import()
commits.body:
- yield was accepted as a plain identifier ENGINE-WIDE, not just in
  patterns: var yield, function yield(){}, function f(yield){},
  if (yield), foo(yield) all parsed. The engine is strict-only, so the
  !is_generator escape hatches that permitted it were wrong everywhere.
  Adds a yield_ok_here flag so yield is also rejected in non-leftmost
  operand position (void yield, 1 + yield, a || yield).
- Escaped keywords are two distinct rules, now separated: a ReservedWord
  spelled with a unicode escape is not that keyword (with an
  as_ident_name opt-out for PropertyName positions), and a legacy octal
  escape in a directive prologue is an early error.
- import/export are legal only at a module's top level. { export var a; }
  and if (1) export var a; were silently ACCEPTED (rc=0) and now reject.
- new import() is not a constructor call. This absorbed the tests filed

early errors at all ([arguments] = [] was accepted in for-of and plain
destructuring assignment); bare for ({...} in o) was collected as a

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject new import() as a constructor call
commits.body:
A NewExpression's callee is a MemberExpression (ES2024 §13.3), and an
ImportCall is a CallExpression — a production MemberExpression does not
derive. `new import('')` is therefore a SyntaxError anywhere it appears, but
new_expression handed the callee straight to member_expr(), which routes a
bare `import` to the dynamic-import path and accepted it.

Reject an `import` token in callee position unless a `.` follows, which keeps
`new import.meta...` on the meta-property path. `new (import(''))` is
unaffected: the parentheses make the call a PrimaryExpression, so it never
reaches this check — as does the covered form
`new (import(''), function () {})`, which test262 pins as valid.

This closes the whole dynamic-import invalid-syntax family (19 tests, spread
across blocks, loops, arrows, and `await` operands in async functions,
arrows and generators).

commits.subject: fix(compiler): restrict import/export to a module's top level
commits.body:
An ImportDeclaration / ExportDeclaration is a ModuleItem (ES2024 §16.2.1), a
production that exists only in a Module's top-level StatementList. Both were
dispatched from the generic statement() switch, so `export` parsed anywhere a
statement could appear: inside a block, a switch case, an if/while/do body, a
labelled statement, a try/catch/finally, and even as a for-loop head, where
`for (export var a;;) ;` sent the parser into an infinite loop rather than an
error.

A new module_top_level flag marks the one dispatch site that may yield a
ModuleItem. compile_module sets it before each top-level statement(), and
statement() consumes it into a local and clears the field on entry, so any
nested statement it parses sees it false. Nested function/arrow contexts get a
fresh CompilerContext and never inherit it. `import(...)` and `import.meta`
are unaffected — they are a CallExpression and a meta-property, routed to
expression_statement before this check.

Separately, the export forms whose grammar ends in `;` used match(SEMICOLON),
which silently tolerates a missing one, so `export {} null;` parsed. The four
non-declaration forms (export default AssignmentExpression, named export,
export star, namespace export) now use expect_semicolon_or_asi. The
HoistableDeclaration / ClassDeclaration forms keep match(SEMICOLON): they end
at their own closing brace and take no semicolon.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject escaped keywords and prologue octal escapes
commits.body:
Two distinct early errors that both surfaced as "escaped keyword" failures.

(a) A ReservedWord is a terminal symbol and must appear literally (ES2024
§5.1.5, §12.7.2), so a spelling using a Unicode escape is neither the keyword
nor a usable Identifier — always a SyntaxError. The lexer already resolved
such a token to its keyword type with has_escape set, but nothing consumed the
flag, so `var x = 1` and `var { break } = {...}` both parsed. The rejection
goes in advance(), the single gate every keyword-consuming path shares. An
IdentifierName position is exempt and passes as_ident_name: object-literal and
class-member keys, plus member accesses, which read via read_property_name
straight off the lexer. So `({ break: 1 })` and `o.break` still parse.

The contextual keywords need the same rule where the grammar demands the
terminal, and they lex as IDENTIFIER so advance() cannot see them:
match_async_method_prefix gains the has_escape bail its two siblings already
had, the object-literal accessor detection ignores escaped `get`/`set`, and
new.target rejects an escaped `target`.

`true`/`false`/`null` are ReservedWords but are not in the keyword table —
they lex as IDENTIFIER and are matched by name in primary_expr. That let
`false` evaluate as the boolean AND let `false:` parse as a labelled
statement. Both now reject; `eval:` / `arguments:` stay valid label names,
since those are not reserved.

(b) A LegacyOctalEscapeSequence is a SyntaxError in strict code (§12.9.4.1).
