commits.subject: fix(compiler): enforce yield binding and precedence restrictions
commits.body:
The engine is strict-only, so `yield` is always a reserved word (ES2024
§13.1.1): never a BindingIdentifier, IdentifierReference, class name, or
label. Several sites carried a `!is_generator` escape hatch that let it be
used as a plain identifier, which is a sloppy-mode-only relaxation this
engine does not have. Remove them from expect_binding_identifier, the var
declarator, function-expression names, class names, and object-literal
shorthand keys, and drop the callers that weakened is_restricted_name's
already-correct default.

Also enforce the positional restriction: a YieldExpression *is* an
AssignmentExpression (§13.15) and derives from nothing tighter, so it is only
legal where the grammar expects one. `yield` was handled in primary_expr, the
bottom of the precedence chain, which wrongly accepted `void yield`,
`1 + yield`, `a || yield` and `yield ? a : b`. A new yield_ok_here flag is set
at the head of assignment_expr and cleared by binary_expr and unary_expr
before every operand that is not the leftmost, so those forms now fail while
`yield + 1`, `x = yield` and `f(yield)` keep parsing.

Fixing `for ({ yield } in o)` surfaced that a bare pattern in a for-in head
was collected with the *param* collectors (declaring VAR leaves), while the
spec makes it an AssignmentPattern exactly like the for-of form. Switch
emit_bare_forin_destruct_loop to the assign collectors and ASSIGN_TARGET, which
also fixes `for ({length: obj.p} in o)` (member targets were a SyntaxError) and
makes the head assign to existing lvalues rather than declaring new ones.
That in turn exposed a pre-existing gap where the array assign collector never
applied the restricted-name early errors at all, so `[arguments] = []` and
`[eval] = []` were accepted in for-of and plain destructuring assignment too;
the check now lives in collect_assign_target, the shared leaf path.

commits.subject: Merge proxy own-keys and generator Catcher lifetime fixes
commits.body:
Two real lifetime bugs, one a hard crash.

proxy_partitioned_own_keys held the ownKeys trap array in a bare local
across N re-entrant getOwnPropertyDescriptor calls, each hitting
safepoints that clear temproots. test/proxy_ownkeys_gc_lifetime.js
SEGFAULTS 3/3 on main (rc=139) and passes 3/3 here; under ASAN it is a
use-after-poison in HObject.array_part. Plain-object for-in under
identical pressure was unaffected, isolating it to the trap path. Fixed
by holding a native frame across the loop.

gs_release drained gs.forin but never gs.cat, so a generator abandoned
while suspended leaked its whole Catcher chain — 1000/1000 leaked, and
the comment claiming the chain is freed with the generator state was
false. Separately mark_generator_state marked every gs field EXCEPT
gs.cat, so an exception parked in a suspended body's finally was rooted
by nothing (removing that mark loses 200/200 parked exceptions).
Ownership is now single-valued: gs.cat is cleared on restore rather than
made symmetric with the deliberate alias. Peak RSS over 400k
abandonments 47.6 MB -> 15.4 MB, matching the exhausted baseline.

vm_reset set act.cat = null WITHOUT freeing, leaking every Catcher an
interrupted run held, and looped only to activation_count. Now frees,
and covers the full MAX_CALLS pool.

Three chain walkers (mark, free, free-nodes-only) collapse into one
catcher_chain_walk, so Catcher.return_val being a borrowed raw copy
while thrown_val is owned is encoded once and cannot drift.

CORRECTION TO da34dda6's MESSAGE: it claimed a pre-fix for-in target was
collectible mid-enumeration and forin_key_still_exists then read freed
memory. The premise holds — instrumentation shows the target loses its
pin and goes unreachable 4x per run — but it is never swept, because
mark_activation_regs scans the whole register span and INITFOR's input
register still names it. The demonstrable claim is 'lost its GC pin and
its only durable root', not 'read freed memory'. The fix remains correct;
only the severity was unsupported.

test262 phases 0-8/11/23/24: 0 regressions across 32750 passing tests.
Local 271 scripts, golden 28/28, forin-rss 98%, new
generator-catcher-rss 100% (reads 310% with the drain removed).

commits.subject: fix(vm): release and mark a suspended generator's Catcher chain
commits.body:
A generator body that suspends inside a try hands its Catcher chain to the
GeneratorState, which is its sole owner while the body sleeps. Nothing ever
freed it: gs_release drained the for-in chain but not the catcher chain, so
a generator abandoned while suspended -- `var it = g(); it.next();`, the
ordinary way to take one value from a lazy sequence -- leaked one Catcher
per instance, plus whatever exception a parked finally still held in
thrown_val. Peak RSS over 400k abandonments: 47.6 MB against 15.3 MB for
the same generator run to exhaustion, 3.1x; with an Error parked on the
chain, 41.9 MB against 9.7 MB. Both are now byte-identical to the baseline.

Instrumenting the single Catcher alloc site against all six free sites put
this precisely: every completion path (return, throw, return-through-finally,
async, nested try) was already balanced at 0 leaked; only the
abandoned-while-suspended path leaked, 1000 of 1000.

The same chain was invisible to the mark phase. mark_activation_fields
marks a running frame's catchers, but mark_generator_state marked every
field on the GeneratorState EXCEPT gs.cat, so an exception parked in a
suspended body's finally was rooted by nothing at all. That is not
theoretical: the regression test loses 200 of 200 parked exceptions with
the mark removed.

Ownership is now single-valued. chains_save_to_gen still ALIASES cat rather
than moving it -- the .throw()/.return() resume paths re-enter the still-live
activation hunting for a catcher, and moving it breaks try/catch inside a
suspended generator -- but chains_restore_from_gen now CLEARS gs.cat, so
while the body runs the activation owns the chain and its pop frees it,
and while it is suspended the gs owns it. Exactly one of the two is
non-null at any time, which is what makes the gs_release drain safe rather
than a double free. Both save/restore macros are renamed from forin_* since
they were never for-in specific.

The heap cannot walk a Catcher (it lives in the vm module, which depends on
heap), so it goes through a CatcherChainFn hook, the same pattern as
mark_activations_fn. Its three modes route through one vm-side walker that
free_catcher_chain and mark_activation_fields also use, so the one place
that knows what a Catcher owns (thrown_val, by tval_copy_ref) versus
borrows (return_val, a raw copy from RET) cannot drift.

vm_reset had the same class of bug twice over: it set act.cat = null
without freeing, leaking every Catcher an interrupted run held, and it
looped only to activation_count. The pool walk is now the full MAX_CALLS.
Frames above the count are drained on the way down today, but that is an
assumption, not an enforced invariant, and MAX_CALLS is a fixed 512-entry
array so covering it costs nothing.

The leak is not observable from script (no GC trigger or heap-stat builtin,
and neither WeakRef nor FinalizationRegistry clears deterministically), so
the memory bound lives in scripts/check_generator_catcher_rss.sh, which
reports 100% of the exhausted-loop baseline and fails at 310% without the
drain. test/generator_catcher_cleanup.js covers the semantics the ownership
change must not break.

commits.subject: fix(proxy): hold a native frame across the own-keys partition loop
commits.body:
proxy_partitioned_own_keys asks the [[OwnPropertyKeys]] trap for an array,
then calls [[GetOwnProperty]] once per key to split it by enumerability.
Each of those calls re-enters the VM, and a nested run hits safepoints,
where GC clears every temproot -- including the pin the freshly allocated
trap result was carrying. The array was reachable only from a C3 local the
mark phase cannot see, so it was collected partway through the loop and the
next arr.array_part()[i] read freed memory.

ASAN reports use-after-poison in HObject.array_part; without ASAN a 50-key
proxy for-in under GC pressure segfaults (exit 139). A plain-object for-in
under identical pressure is unaffected, which is what isolates it to the
trap path.

The fix is the guard builtin_dispatch already takes around every builtin
handler: bump native_frame_depth for the duration, which vetoes the
temproot clear. The keys read out of the array are covered by the same
window -- they are strings the trap built and nothing else names, and
sweep_strings frees an interned string that is unreachable with refcount 1,
so interning does not root them either.

test/proxy_ownkeys_gc_lifetime.js covers for-in, Object.keys,
getOwnPropertyNames, the non-enumerable partition, and keys held across a
generator suspend. It segfaults without the fix and passes with it.

commits.subject: Merge destructuring pattern early errors
commits.body:
Four sub-rules, all cases of the engine accepting patterns it must
reject:

- A reserved word as an object shorthand target ({if} = x), including
  the unicode-escaped spelling. 78 tests.
- yield as a shorthand target. 2 tests.
- An elision or trailing comma after a rest element ([...r,] = x).
  4 tests.
- eval/arguments as a pattern target. 3 tests.

The eval/arguments check landed in collect_assign_target, the single
choke point for leaf targets, so it covers array elements, object
properties, rest targets and arbitrary nesting in one place rather than
N — the recurring lesson being that an invariant maintained in N places
is wrong in the copies that omit it. The same 'while (self.match(COMMA))'
idiom appeared in three collectors and was wrong in all three.

87 newly passing, 0 regressions. Phase 2 2172 -> 2215 (84 -> 41 fail),
phase 11 390 -> 429 (43 -> 4 fail), phases 0 and 3 unchanged. Local
suite 270 scripts, golden 28/28.

test/destructuring_early_errors.js is 96/96 here, fails on main, and
runs UNMODIFIED under node with an identical 96/96 — expectations are
V8-verified rather than engine-matching. A separate 14-case accept
table of valid destructuring forms is byte-identical to node, so
nothing valid became rejected.

Scope correction from the agent: the family is 106 dstr-path failures,
not the 192 I estimated, and the residual 19 are NOT a destructuring
bug — yield is accepted as a plain identifier engine-wide (var yield,
function yield(){}, function f(yield){} all parse; node rejects all
three). That belongs to the yield-binding family.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): enforce destructuring pattern early errors
commits.body:
Four early-error rules were under-enforced: the engine accepted source
the spec requires it to reject. All are fixed at the point the parser
already knows the context, extending existing checks rather than adding
parallel ones.

1. A reserved word may be a property *key* (`{extends: t}`) but not the
   shorthand *target* (`{extends}`), where the key doubles as an
   IdentifierReference / BindingIdentifier. The object-*literal* path
   already got this right; the pattern collectors route reserved words
   through destructuring_property_key, which hands back the keyword's
   spelling as a plain char[], so the existing is_restricted_name check
   (strict-mode restrictions only) never saw a reserved word. Adds the
   shared shorthand_key_is_identifier_ref predicate and applies it in
   both the assignment- and binding-pattern collectors. Escaped
   spellings (`{ var }`) come along for free: ES2024 §12.6.1 makes
   the lexer resolve an escaped reserved word to its keyword token.

2. `yield` is a reserved word in strict code regardless of generator
   context. This engine is strict-only, so the `!is_generator &&
   !forbid_yield` idiom (which encodes the sloppy-mode allowance) is
   unreachable and the shorthand target is always rejected.

3. A rest element must be last. `while (self.match(COMMA)) {}` silently
   swallowed anything following it, so `[...x,]` and `{...a,}` parsed.
   Replaced with a check in all three collectors (array/object binding,
   array assignment). A trailing comma without a rest stays legal.

4. A pattern's leaf assignment target must be a valid simple assignment
   target, so `[eval] = v` is rejected exactly as the non-pattern
   `eval = v` already was. Added in collect_assign_target, the single
   point every leaf target passes through, plus the shorthand branch of
   the binding collector which omitted the is_restricted_name check its
   `{key: target}` sibling had.

`yield` as a general *expression* (`[x = yield]`, `[x[yield]]`), which
reproduces with no pattern present at all (`var x = yield;`) and is an
engine-wide gap, not a destructuring one.

print shim) and reports identical counts, so the expectations are
V8-verified.

commits.subject: Merge GETPROPC2 proxy write-back and chain-fusion jump guard
commits.body:
The hop-2 Proxy path returned before writing the hop-1 result back into
the intermediate temp, which every other exit path does. This was filed
as latent on the reasoning that the compiler cannot emit a chain whose
temp is read after a proxied second hop. That reasoning was wrong — it
considered value reads and missed the RECEIVER reload. Three lines of
ordinary JavaScript reproduce it:

  var target = { z: function(){ return this === p ? 'proxy-this' : 'target-this'; } };
  var p = new Proxy(target, { get: function(t,k){ return t[k]; } });
  var o = { m: p };
  o.m.z()      // was 'target-this', node says 'proxy-this'

o.m.z() reloads the temp as the call's `this`, so a proxied first hop
invoked the method with the wrong receiver. Note reachability is decided
by register allocation, not source shape — a near-identical script
passes because the temp coincidentally already held the proxy.

Also makes fuse_getpropc_chains consult the shared jump-target bitset,
the last peephole that did not. Measured over 47562 corpus files: 33399
fusions fire, zero data slots are branch destinations, and a wholesale
disasm diff shows zero files' bytecode changes — the guard rejects
nothing today. Kept because the invariant it replaces was an unenforced
property of other code, and three bugs of exactly this shape were found
in this file's neighbours this session.

run_golden_bytecode.py's FUSED_OPCODES is an exact name-set
intersection, so GETPROPC was not covering GETPROPC2 — the
--check-noop disable_optimize invariant had a hole for this opcode.

Differential vs node 15 cases (revoked proxies, revoke-mid-chain,
throwing and side-effecting traps, GC-heavy traps, proxies on both
hops, IC-warm loops): 5/15 wrong before, 0 after. test262 phases
0-8/11/23 unchanged across 31676 tests; Proxy 262/0. Golden 27/27 ->
28/28, no existing .expected regenerated. Local suite 269 scripts.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): make the GETPROPC2 chain fusion consult the jump-target bitset
commits.body:
fuse_getpropc_chains was the only peephole that rewrote slot i+1 without
checking whether it is a branch destination. That slot stops being a decodable
instruction — the VM reads the second hop's destination and key out of it and
skips past — so control arriving there from a jump would decode a data word.
Safety rested entirely on the compiler never branching into the middle of a
two-hop property chain, which nothing enforced.

Now it uses the shared build_jump_targets bitset, like every other fusion pass.

Cost: none. Instrumenting the pass and compiling all 47562 test262 language/
and built-ins/ files: 33399 fusions fire, ZERO have a jump target on the data
slot (and zero alias r_tmp with the hop-2 destination). A wholesale disasm diff
of both compilers over the same 47562 files reports 0 files whose bytecode
changes, so the guard rejects no fusion that exists today. Interleaved 15-rep
A/B on the property-heavy benchmarks is within the A/A noise floor (a single
10ms timer tick); no measurable delta.

The check is kept despite costing nothing to reject, because the alternative is
a silent miscompile the day codegen puts a label, loop head or join between the
hops. Three bugs of this exact shape (073aa16b, 4f486724, and the WIDE-format
gap in 329bc73a) were found in neighbouring passes.

Also adds GETPROPC2 to FUSED_OPCODES in the golden runner: the --check-noop
invariant is an exact name-set intersection, so "GETPROPC" did not cover it and
the fused opcode could have leaked into --no-optimize output unnoticed.

failures — all the engine accepting syntax it must reject. This closes
the three cheapest families.

  the Pratt loop, at the ternary join, per comma operand, and in the
  arithmetic/logical unary cases.

  prologue is an early error when the parameter list has a rest element,
  default initializer or destructuring pattern. Needed two fixes beyond
  the check: arrow block bodies never parsed a directive prologue at

  function f(a=1) { "use strict" } was missed.

resumed with prev_tt hard-coded to SEMICOLON after a declarator with an
initializer, putting the initializer at statement position. Harmless
before, but the new duplicate check turned it into a rejection of the

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject duplicate lexical declarations in a block
commits.body:
ES2024 §13.2.1 makes it an early SyntaxError for the LexicallyDeclaredNames of
a BlockStatement to contain duplicate entries. let, const, class and
FunctionDeclaration all contribute lexical names, but only let/const/class went
through the declaration-site duplicate check in var_declaration — function
declarations never touch scope_stack, so `{ function f(){} class f{} }`,
`{ let x; function x(){} }` and `{ function f(){} function* f(){} }` were all
accepted.

The block pre-scan already collects every one of these names for TDZ
initialisation, so the check goes there: one pairwise scan over the names the
pre-scan returned, rather than a second mechanism alongside the existing one.

§B.3.2.1 relaxes the rule for exactly one pair — two PLAIN FunctionDeclarations
may share a name in a block. It does not extend to `function*` or
`async function`, so NameSpan carries a redeclarable_fn bit set only for a
plain declaration; every other combination collides. The check is limited to
genuine BlockStatements, since a function body's top-level function
declarations are var-scoped and legitimately redeclarable.

Fixes a latent bug in the same pre-scan found while testing this: after a
declarator with an initializer the scan resumed with prev_tt hard-coded to
SEMICOLON, putting the initializer at statement position. A named class or
function EXPRESSION there was then collected as a block-level binding, so the
new duplicate check rejected the valid `let x = class x {}`. prev_tt now
carries the actual separator.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject "use strict" in a non-simple parameter list's body
commits.body:
ES2024 §15.2.1 (and the parallel clauses for generators, async functions,
methods and arrows) make it an early SyntaxError for a function body to carry
a "use strict" directive when IsSimpleParameterList of its FormalParameters is
false — that is, when any parameter is a rest element, has an initializer, or
is a destructuring pattern.

The engine is strict-only and accepts the directive as a no-op, so nothing
downstream depended on it and the early error never fired. Add it in
parse_directives, where the directive is already recognised, gated on a new
params_are_simple() reading the three signals the parameter loops record.

Two supporting fixes were needed for the check to cover every function form:

- has_destructured_param is set inside collect_obj_param_binds /
  collect_arr_param_binds rather than at the twelve call sites in the three
  parameter loops, gated on in_formal_params because those functions are
  shared with statement destructuring.
- Arrow block bodies never called parse_directives at all, so they had no
  directive prologue; `(a = 1) => { "use strict"; }` bypassed the check
  entirely. Both arrow compile paths now parse one.

Also treat the `}` closing a body as ending a directive: ASI terminates the
ExpressionStatement there, so `function f(a=1) { "use strict" }` (no trailing
semicolon) has a directive prologue and must be rejected too.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject invalid AssignmentTargetType early
commits.body:
An operator's result is a value, never a Reference, so it can never be an
assignment target (ES2024 §13.15.1). The parser tracks "the expression just
parsed was a Reference" with last_was_getvar / last_was_member /
last_was_local_var, and assignment_expr already rejected an LHS with none of
them set — but no operator ever cleared them. They therefore described the
operator's last OPERAND rather than its result, so `x + y = 1` was accepted
and compiled to an assignment to `y`, and `(a === b) = 1` to one to `b`.

Clear the markers where each production's value is produced: after the Pratt
loop in binary_expr (covering all four operator forms, including the
short-circuit ones), at the ternary join in conditional_expr, on each comma
operand in expression(), and in the four arithmetic/logical unary cases.
Clearing inside the binary loop instead would not work — every form parses its
right operand afterwards and that parse re-sets the flags from its own last
operand.

The three markers move together via clear_ref_markers() rather than being
cleared field-by-field at each site, so a future production cannot clear some
and leave a stale one to slip through.

commits.subject: Merge for-in enumeration state ownership
commits.body:
for (k in o) break; leaked the ForInState and left the target
permanently temproot-pinned: cleanup existed only on the exhausted
NEXTFOR path, with nothing on any unwind edge. 200k iterations took
111 MB against 2.2 MB for the same loop run to completion, and the
pinned target was never collectible — unbounded in long-running code.

Owned on the activation, in two layers: INITFOR releases whatever its
own output register still names (bounding the loop idiom, which leaks
within a single frame and so cannot be caught by frame teardown), and
free_forin_chain catches anything surviving to the pop. The drain is
folded INTO free_catcher_chain rather than added as a parallel call at
its 7 sites — a second call is a second thing to forget, which is the
failure mode behind most of this session's bugs. Generators save and
restore the chain across suspend/resume, so a for-in can yield
mid-enumeration.

Two pre-existing bugs surfaced under ASAN and are fixed here. The
serious one: ForInState was invisible to the GC and the temproot pin is
NOT durable — mark_and_sweep clears every temproot at a safepoint
(heap.c3:3090). A for-in whose target was referenced nowhere else was
collectible mid-enumeration, after which forin_key_still_exists read
freed memory. Baseline avoided crashing only because the leak meant
nothing dereferenced the stale target on the abandoned path.

the exhausted loop), return 58.3 -> 3.7, throw 64.1 -> 9.5,
labeled-continue 58.3 -> 3.7, labeled-break 58.3 -> 3.7, nested

commits.subject: fix(vm): own for-in enumeration state on the activation
commits.body:
`for (k in o) break;` — the standard "is this object non-empty" idiom —
leaked one ForInState per iteration and left the enumerated object
temproot-pinned forever. 200k iterations cost 112 MB against 3.7 MB for
the same loop run to exhaustion.

Cleanup lived only on the exhausted path in NEXTFOR. Every abrupt exit
(break, labeled break, return, a propagating throw, a labeled continue to
an outer loop) stranded the state, and the compiler frees the iter_state
register after the loop so nothing could reach it again.

Rather than emit a free at each exit edge — the same hand-maintained
invariant that produced 073aa16b, 0ee9fd78 and 4f486724, each of which was
"correct in N places and wrong in the copies that omitted it" — ownership
moves to the frame:

  - Activation.forin is an intrusive ForInState chain, exactly like
    Activation.cat. INITFOR pushes; the register only borrows.
  - free_catcher_chain drains it, so all seven existing frame-pop sites
    get for-in cleanup without naming it. One function, not two calls.
  - INITFOR releases whatever its own output register still names, which
    is what bounds the loop idiom within a single frame.
  - A suspending generator MOVES the chain onto its GeneratorState
    (forin_save_to_gen) and takes it back on resume; gs_release frees an
    abandoned one. Freeing at the suspend pop would be a use-after-free,
    since saved_regs still names the state.
  - vm_complete_generator_return drains directly: its pop is final and
    deliberately skips the catcher chain (still aliased by gs.cat).

Two latent bugs surfaced under ASAN while fixing this:

  - ForInState was invisible to the GC and the temproot pin is NOT
    durable — mark_and_sweep clears every temproot at a safepoint. A
    for-in whose target was referenced nowhere else could be swept
    mid-enumeration, after which NEXTFOR's liveness re-check read freed
    memory. mark_activation_fields and mark_generator_state now mark the
    chain's targets.
  - vm_complete_generator_return popped without releasing frame-owned
    state, so a generator closed by .return() mid-for-in leaked one state
    per instance (deterministic, 400/400 under LeakSanitizer).

Activation.max_heap_reg moves next to `flags` so the two uints share an
8-byte slot: Activation[MAX_CALLS] is copied to a 64 Kb-capped stack local
on three re-entrant paths, and the new field would otherwise overflow it.

Peak RSS, 200k iterations: break 112,836,608 -> 3,686,400 bytes, now
byte-identical to the exhausted loop. return/throw/labeled-break/
labeled-continue/nested/proxy all bounded.

Duplicate now deleted in favour of the shared helper.

produces a wrong value, because fusion_abc_reads_reg over-approximates
CALL's C field (an argc, not a register) and independently pins the same
register live. Two bugs cancel. Both sites now say so in comments —
widening that CALL carve-out, an obvious future optimization, would make
this latent bug observable.

run_jmp_lt_g_fusion) are both SOUND. fuse_getpropc_chains is sound only

commits.subject: fix(compiler): liveness scan must not read a branch offset as a register
commits.body:
Audit of every fusion/peephole in compiler/fusion.c3, context.c3,
moveelim.c3 and peephole.c3 for the class "reasons about a neighbouring
instruction by position and opcode without checking which register it
reads, or whether a branch can land between slots assumed contiguous".

One real defect, in the SHARED helper rather than in a caller.
fusion_reg_live_from ended its dead-after scan on `jns.a == reg` for
every instruction format. WIDE_SABC/WIDE_ABC (JUMP/BREAK/CONTINUE) have
no A field: they pack a 24-bit signed offset across A/B/C, so A is the
offset's LOW BYTE. `JUMP +3` therefore looked exactly like a write to
register 3 and ended the scan, reporting a still-live register dead —
the unsafe direction, since it PERMITS a fusion whose scratch value is
read again later. The function's own doc comment already asserted that
WIDE operands "must not be misread as" register references; the code
did not implement it.

Same shape as the three bugs already fixed this session: the two copies
of this scan that carried the guard (cmp_result_live_from,
run_move_gg_fusion's private loop) were correct, and the shared copy
that omitted it was the buggy one. Fixed once in the shared helper, and
run_move_gg_fusion's hand-copied loop is deleted in favour of calling it
— a duplicated liveness scan is how the guard came to be missing.

Reachability measured, not assumed: instrumenting the scan and compiling
all 47291 test262 language/ and built-ins/ files showed 212 scans
stopping on this alias (211 JUMP, 1 BREAK), and 17 files' fused bytecode
changes once guarded. No input is known to produce a wrong VALUE, because
fusion_abc_reads_reg independently over-approximates CALL's C field (an
argc, not a register) and pins the same register live; the two errors
cancel. That cancellation is now documented at both sites so widening
either one cannot silently turn latent into observable.

Sound-but-only-accidentally cases documented rather than changed:
- fuse_getpropc_chains (peephole.c3) reasons purely positionally with no
  jump-target bitset. Sound only because the compiler never branches
  into the middle of a two-hop chain (0 hits over 47291 files) and
  because the GETPROPC2 handler writes the intermediate temp back — the
  temp is live after the pair in 5232 files, so the pass cannot rely on
  it being dead. The hop-2 Proxy path returns before that write-back;
  latent today, noted.
- run_cmp_branch_fusion's bridge_slot/skip_tgt reject out-of-range
  backward targets via unsigned wraparound, not an explicit >= 0 test.
- fusion_reg_live_from is a linear scan, not a CFG walk: it can only
  over-report liveness, which suppresses fusions but never permits an
  unsafe one.

commits.body:
The runner skipped every test carrying $DONOTEVALUATE, which meant
4310 negative:phase:parse tests never ran — the tests that verify the
engine REJECTS bad syntax. The suite validated what we accept and said
nothing about what we must refuse. That is why the arrow
duplicate-parameter bug shipped: params-duplicate.js existed, reported
FAIL via --single, and the suite read 0 fails.

The skip now runs LAST and un-skips only negative:phase:parse, so tests
excluded by feature token or noStrict stay excluded. 50446 -> 54643
tests run, 4197 newly visible, zero regressions across all 23 phases.

Also fixes a real bug the new coverage exposed: a declaration in
single-statement body position was accepted. `if (true) let x = 1;`,
`while (false) const y = 1;` and `lbl: class C {}` all parsed clean;
node rejects them. New statement_body() gates the 11 body call sites
(if/else, while, do-while, for x3, for-in/of x4, label x2); block() and
switch_statement() stay on statement() since declarations are legal
there. That turned 89 of the newly-visible failures green.

Phase 11 alone: 312 pass / 153 skip -> 386 pass / 47 fail / 32 skip,
with 74 newly passing and zero previously-passing tests lost.

The remaining 765 newly-visible failures are all the engine accepting
source it must reject, triaged into 11 early-error families (192
destructuring, 102 yield-binding, 97 lexical redeclaration, 74
AssignmentTargetType, 56 module syntax, 55 escaped keywords, 32
use-strict-with-non-simple-params, and a tail). Each is a
self-contained follow-up; none are skip-worthy.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): reject declarations in single-statement body position
commits.body:
Only a StatementList (a block, function body, case clause, or the top level)
may contain a Declaration. The body of an if/else, a loop, or a label admits
Statement but not StatementListItem, so `if (x) class C {}`,
`while (0) function f(){}` and `for(;;) const x = 1;` are early SyntaxErrors.

The compiler used one statement() for both positions, so every declaration
form was silently accepted as a bare body. Add statement_body() for the
Statement-only positions and route the 11 body call sites through it; block()
and switch_statement() keep statement() because those are StatementLists.

`let` only counts as a declaration when a binding actually follows, so the
guard reports the accurate error rather than a generic parse failure.

Fixes 89 test262 tests, 0 regressions.

commits.body:

covered 4604 files. $DONOTEVALUATE tells the harness not to RUN a file; it
is not a reason not to COMPILE it. A `negative: phase: parse` test asserts
the engine REJECTS the source, and that is verified entirely by compiling —
the worker already maps a compile error on such a test to a pass.

Skipping them left the engine's whole parse-rejection surface unmeasured.

and the suite read zero failures because it was skipped.

and agent-harness rules still own the tests they exclude; un-skipping
parse-negatives cannot resurrect a test another rule already excludes. The
33 `phase: resolution` module-linking tests need the loader rather than the
parser and stay skipped.

commits.subject: Merge operand-value preservation fixes
commits.body:
Two evaluation-order bugs, both about an operand's VALUE surviving a
later assignment.

  (w=2)*(w=3) returned 9, node 6; (x=2)+(x=3) returned 6, node 5
  g=5; g += (g=2) returned 4, node 7; g -= (g=2) returned 0, node 3

binary_expr's single copy-to-temp block conflated two concerns:
choosing a safe DESTINATION for the result, and preserving the left
operand's VALUE across the right operand's evaluation. It only ever did
the former, and ran after the right operand was already emitted.

I attempted this myself first by moving that block earlier. That breaks
the engine: it changes which register receives the result, so
fib(n-1) went from SUBI r3 = r0, r1 to SUBI r0 = r0, r1 and destroyed
the parameter — fib(10) returned 6. A 21-case value differential
against node passed 20/21 and gave no signal; only the golden-bytecode
diffs exposed it.

The fix keeps destination selection exactly as it was and adds a
SECOND, separately-gated copy that materializes the left value before
the right operand compiles, guarded by a bounded token scan for
assignment operators. Deciding before allocating is what makes it work:
alloc_reg is a bump allocator, so a speculative copy cannot be
retracted without renumbering every later register.

The compound branch of assignment_expr gets the same treatment for the
target's old value. Member targets (o.p +=, a[0] +=) already went
through PUTPROP correctly and are pinned by assertions so the
local-only gating cannot silently start applying to them.

Bug A matrix 306 cases: 106 wrong -> 0. Bug B matrix 414 cases
including short-circuit &&=/||=/??=: 27 wrong -> 0. Golden bytecode
26/26 with ZERO churn. test262 phases 0-8 unchanged. Emitted bytecode
compared across all 288 files under benchmarks/ and test/ — only the
edited test file differs, so runtime cost is provably zero and
t = t + 1 still fuses to a single ADDI.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): read a compound assignment's target before its RHS
commits.body:
`g op= rhs` is: resolve the Reference for g, GetValue(g) -> old, evaluate rhs,
apply op(old, rhs), PutValue. The read of g happens first. assignment_expr
compiled the RHS first and only then applied the op to g's home register,
which the RHS had already overwritten:

    function f(){ var g=5; g += (g=2); return g; }   // 4, node says 7
    function h(){ var g=5; g -= (g=2); return g; }   // 0, node says 3

computing 2 + 2 instead of 5 + 2. The old value is now copied to a temp before
the RHS is compiled, and the compound op reads that temp.

Independent of the left-operand fix in the preceding commit (that one is about
a binary operator's left operand; this one is the op-assign branch), but gated
on the same conservative rhs_may_write_registers() lookahead, so a RHS that
cannot write a register emits unchanged code.

Scoped to plain local targets: member targets (o.p, q[0]) go through PUTPROP
and already re-read correctly, and the logical forms (&&=, ||=, ??=) return
earlier because they must short-circuit and not evaluate the RHS at all —
covered by explicit skip/take assertions.

414-case differential (15 compound operators x 3 RHS kinds x 3 target kinds x
3 contexts, plus logical short-circuit initial values) vs node: 27 cases wrong
before, 0 after. test/codegen_assign_clobber.js grows to 36 assertions, all
cross-checked against node; a baseline build fails 14 of them.

Verification that the change is free: with both binaries built with tracing,
the emitted bytecode of all 288 files under benchmarks/ and test/ was compared
and only codegen_assign_clobber.js differs — the file these cases were added
to. `just test-golden-bytecode` stays 26/26 with no churn, and every benchmark
compiles byte-identically, so the bench-fast wobble is measurement noise.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): preserve left operand's value across the right operand
commits.body:
`a op b` must use a's value as of before b runs — the spec evaluates
GetValue(lref) before b. When `left` was a live local's home register and b
assigned that same variable, b overwrote the value in place:

    function f(){ var w; return (w=2)*(w=3); }   // 9, node says 6
    function h(){ var x; return (x=2)+(x=3); }   // 6, node says 5

    LDINT r0, +2      ; w = 2
    LDINT r0, +3      ; w = 3   -- clobbers the left operand
    MUL   r1 = r0, r0 ; 3 * 3

binary_expr's existing copy-to-temp ran *after* the right operand was already
parsed and emitted. Its job is choosing a destination register the RESULT can
safely land in, and it has to stay where it is: it consumes the register the
right operand just released, so hoisting it earlier reassigns the result
register and destroys parameters (`n - 1` in `fib` becomes `SUBI r0 = r0, r1`,
overwriting `n`; fib(10) returns 6).

So this adds a *second*, separately gated copy for the left operand's VALUE,
emitted before the right operand. It fires only when the right operand can
actually write a register, decided by rhs_may_write_registers() — a
conservative raw-token scan (assignment ops, ++/--) over a saved/restored
lexer. Over-approximating is safe: a false positive costs one LDREG in a rare
shape, a false negative is a miscompile. Ordinary code is untouched, so
`just test-golden-bytecode` stays 26/26 with no churn and `t = t + 1` in a
loop still fuses to a single ADDI with no dead LDREG.

Enables the known-failure assertion in test/codegen_assign_clobber.js and adds
coverage for same-var-on-the-right, chaining, loops, compound and update RHS.
All 21 assertions cross-checked against node.

cases wrong before, 0 after. test262 phases 0-8 PASS sets diffed with comm:

commits.subject: fix(compiler): apply FormalParameters early errors to arrow params
commits.body:
`compile_arrow_inner_reparse` is the third parameter-list prologue, and
unlike `parse_function_body` and `compile_inner_function` it performed
neither the restricted-name check nor the duplicate-BoundName check. So
every arrow escaped ES2015 §14.2.1 validation:

    (a, a) => a        no throw   (SyntaxError)
    (eval) => 1        no throw   (SyntaxError)
    (arguments) => 1   no throw   (SyntaxError)
    (a, ...a) => 1     no throw   (SyntaxError)

while the identical function forms were correctly rejected.

Rather than add a fourth hand-rolled copy of the check, collect the
seen-names table and the two early errors into a `SeenParams` type and
call it from all three prologues. A prologue can no longer record a bound
name without validating it, which is the invariant the arrow copy lost.

This also fixes a duplicate-name hole all three prologues shared:
destructured leaves were never checked, so `function f([a], {a})` and
`([a], {a}) => 1` both compiled. Patterns are collected into a flat array
as the list is parsed, so they are validated in one sweep once the whole
list is known — a pattern can collide with a simple parameter in either
order.

The arrow prologue also used a bare `expect(IDENTIFIER)` where the other
two use `expect_binding_identifier()`; switching it lets `await`/`yield`
be accepted as arrow parameter names exactly where the enclosing grammar
still permits them as identifiers, instead of failing later with a
misleading "expected ';'" error.

Verified against node: 31 differential cases (duplicates, restricted
names, destructured duplicates, async arrows, nested arrows, arrows in
class bodies, rest/default params) now all match, with no over-rejection
of legitimate parameter lists or body-level shadowing.

commits.subject: Merge GC fix: mark a closure's whole scope chain, not just the innermost link
commits.body:
Not an async bug — async was only how it became observable. An
EnvRecord is pool-allocated and never collected, but its bindings field
is an ordinary GC heap node, and every object-graph marking site rooted
only the first link it could reach. None walked EnvRecord.parent.

A closure over outer -> middle -> inner survived a sweep with
inner.bindings intact and outer.bindings recycled into the object pool,
so the first GETVAR walking past inner read a freed block. Surfaced as
use-after-poison in get_shape <- find_prop_idx <- Vm.run <-
drain_microtasks, the same ASAN signature as 6c67835d but a different
victim: the dead chain belonged to a closure the NEXT microtask was
about to invoke.

mark_activation_envs (vm_core.c3:24-35) has always done the full walk
and documents why — 'keep all enclosing scopes alive'. The object-graph
marker never got that treatment, which is exactly why only closures
resumed after a GC could hit it and a frame live across one never
could.

New Heap.mark_env_chain() walks to the root; the six single-link
.bindings marks now use it, with the ownership rule stated: whoever
roots a scope chain roots the whole chain, and callers must never mark
env.bindings directly. The remaining single-link mark (VarIC cache)
holds a direct bindings pointer, not a chain, and is correctly
unchanged.

test/env_chain_gc_lifetime.js is 161/161 here (stable 3/3) and 40/160
on main. ASAN on test_async_loops.js: use-after-poison at
hobject.c3:910 before, clean PASS after. Phases 24/8/7 unchanged

commits.body:

Vm.run <- drain_microtasks on test/test_async_loops.js under ASAN.

Same crash signature as the async-resume UAF fixed in 6c67835d, but a
distinct bug and not an async one at all. Tracing the victim through the
sweep: the freed block was an EnvRecord.bindings object, swept with
reachable=0 and no temproot, and the crash-time env walk reached it as the
THIRD link of a chain (c178 -> c268 -> 001618). The activation live at that
GC had a different, fully-marked chain — the dead chain belonged to a
closure the next microtask was about to invoke.

The ownership defect: an EnvRecord is pool-allocated and never collected,
but its `bindings` is an ordinary heap node, and every object-graph marking
site rooted only the FIRST link it could reach —

  heap.c3 drain_gray  FUNCTION:  func.var_env.bindings, func.lex_env.bindings
  heap.c3 drain_gray  GENERATOR: gen.var_env.bindings,  gen.lex_env.bindings
  heap.c3 mark_generator_state:  gs.var_env,            gs.lex_env

none of which walked EnvRecord.parent. A closure captured over
`outer -> middle -> inner` therefore survived a sweep with inner.bindings
intact and outer.bindings freed and recycled into the object pool; the first
GETVAR that walked past `inner` read the recycled block.

mark_activation_envs (vm_core.c3) has always done the full parent walk, and
documents why ("keep all enclosing scopes alive"). That is precisely why the
bug only ever bit closures resumed AFTER a GC — async bodies, .then handlers
and generator resumes — and never a frame that was live across it.

Fix at the ownership level: Heap.mark_env_chain walks the chain to the root,
and all six sites use it. No new roots are introduced (it only extends an
existing traversal over pointers the chain already holds), so it cannot
retain anything that was not already referenced; LeakSanitizer is clean on
the async/generator/promise corpus. Added env_record_parent alongside the
existing env_record_bindings, since heap.c3 cannot import env.c3.

mark_activation_envs are redundant with the full walk right below them.

commits.body:

commits.subject: fix(compiler): bridge correction must require the continuation to read rA
commits.body:
`for (var j = 0; j < n; j++) { if (j) { r += '2' } else { r += '3' } }`
returned "333" instead of "322" — silent wrong output, no error, no crash.

run_cmp_branch_fusion's bridge correction (fusion.c3) extended the fused
offset past ANY forward IF_FALSE/IF_TRUE sitting at the branch target,
on the assumption that such a branch is always an `&&`/`||`
continuation. It checked only the opcode and the sign of the offset,
never which register the candidate reads.

The correction exists because a genuine continuation re-tests rA — the
compare's own result register, which the fusion stops materializing —
and would otherwise see a stale value. A forward branch on any OTHER
register is unrelated; skipping past it deletes a real instruction from
the taken path.

A loop whose body starts with a bare truthiness test on a
register-resident local is exactly that shape: the back-edge target is
an `IF_FALSE rJ`, so the correction fired on the loop's own body top and
moved the back-edge one branch deeper, into the else arm. Every
iteration after the first re-executed only that arm, which is why a
countdown loop yielded a constant "333" rather than an off-by-one. Only
bare truthiness was affected — `if (j !== 0)`, `if (!j)` and `if (j &&
1)` all emit something between the condition and the branch.

The condition is now `code[bridge_slot].a == rA`. The NOP-compaction
remap in context.c3 was correct throughout; the wrong offset was baked
in before it ran.

commits.subject: Merge three independent fixes: generator this, throw reporting, --no-optimize
commits.body:
- ES5 10.4.3 this-substitution was missing for dynamically-constructed
  generators: GeneratorFunction('yield this')().next().value gave
  undefined where node gives the global. The omission was at generator
  CREATION, not the resume path — GEN_START snapshots this_binding into
  gs.this_binding and every resume restores that snapshot, so a bad
  receiver self-propagates. Async generators reach this by a different
  path and were already correct. Source-declared generators correctly
  continue not to substitute.

- Uncaught throws of non-Error values printed 'VM error: vm::VM_ERROR
  (at execute)', misreporting a JS throw as an internal engine fault —
  the same wording that signals a real fault, so the two were
  indistinguishable. Format the thrown value instead, and reserve the
  VM error wording for a genuine internal fault. Exit code for these
  goes 0 -> 1, matching the Error case.

- --no-optimize emitted no code at all: the !disable_optimize guard
  wrapped the only site assigning func.code/func.code_count, so the
  disable_optimize branches inside it were dead. This also meant
  --check-noop had been passing vacuously — an empty disassembly
  trivially contains no fused opcodes.

Note documented in AGENTS.md: local-var-to-register elision is
load-bearing for CORRECTNESS, not just speed. Under --no-optimize a
function-local var resolves against the global env and leaks outward,

commits.subject: fix(compiler): don't rewrite a ternary's join across the branch
commits.body:
A conditional expression used as the RIGHT operand of a binary operator
evaluated the FALSE branch regardless of the condition — silently, with no
error and no crash. `5 + (true ? 10 : 20)` yielded 25 instead of 15.

Two independent peepholes both rewrote the ternary's join point without
noticing it was a join point:

1. Copy propagation (context.c3) collapsed `LDREG rT=rS ; ADD rD=rD,rT`
   into `ADD rD=rD,rS` and NOP'd the move. For a ternary that LDREG IS the
   false arm's join copy: each arm computes into its own scratch rS and
   copies into the shared result rT. The true arm's JUMP lands directly on
   the consumer having written rT and never rS, so it read the false arm's
   leftover scratch. The pass's comment asserted this was safe because "rS
   is the actual variable" — true for the loop-body copies it was written
   for, false for a per-arm temp.

2. LDINT+ADD -> ADDI fusion (fusion.c3, run_fusion_rule) baked the false
   arm's literal into the join instruction as an immediate, so both arms
   got 20. `run_fusion_rule` was documented as not needing jump-target
   safety at all; that reasoning only covered the trigger slot, not the
   consumer.

Both now consult a jump-target bitset and decline to rewrite when the
consumer slot is a branch destination. The bitset builder is factored out
as `build_jump_targets` — three fusion passes carried byte-identical
private copies of it, and the two passes that lacked one are exactly the
two that were wrong.

The LDREG slot itself being a jump target is deliberately NOT rejected:
those are loop back-edges onto a body whose source register is a live
local, and guarding them costs the `total = total + i` copy elision that
golden_bytecode/loop_addi pins, with no correctness gain.

Verified: 2910-case differential matrix against node
({+,-,*,/,%,**,<<,>>,>>>,&,|,^,<,>,<=,>=,==,===,!=,!==,&&,||,??,concat}
x {ternary left/right/both, nested, chained, side-effecting arms,
compound assignment, loop conditions} x {literal true, literal false,
computed}) is byte-identical to node; 95 cases were wrong before.

28776 passing tests. just test-local 255+12 green.
just test-golden-bytecode 10/10 with no golden file regenerated.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): --no-optimize emitted no code at all and segfaulted
commits.body:
`./out/duktape_c3_debug --no-optimize <file>` exited 139 on every input,
including an empty file, defeating the AGENTS.md-documented technique for
isolating peephole/optimizer bugs.

Root cause is not in the peepholes: the NOP-compaction block in
CompilerContext.finish() was guarded by `!self.disable_optimize`, but its
Step 4 is the ONLY place func.code / func.code_count are ever assigned. So
--no-optimize skipped code emission entirely, leaving every CompiledFunction
with a null code pointer, and the VM jumped through it. The
disable_optimize branches inside that block (the verbatim-copy path) were
written for exactly this case but were unreachable behind the outer guard.

Guard on code_count alone and gate Steps 1-3 (which only compact NOPs and
remap offsets) individually; Step 4 already handles both modes. The diff is
four small edits — the line count is re-indentation of the inner block.

--no-optimize now runs correctly and its disassembly shows the unfused
stream (LDINT/LDINT/ADD where the optimized build fuses ADDI), which is
what the technique needs.

Note the golden-bytecode --check-noop invariant was passing VACUOUSLY: it
asserts fused opcodes are absent, and the disassembly was empty. It is only
now a real assertion (still 10/10).

Surfaced, NOT fixed here: local-var-to-register elision is load-bearing for
correctness, not just speed. With it disabled a function-local `var` emits
DECLVAR_HOIST/DECLVAR/PUTVAR, which resolve against the GLOBAL environment,
so an inner `var x` leaks to the outer scope. Three test/ files fail under
--no-optimize for this reason. Documented in AGENTS.md with a minimal repro
so the flag is not mistaken for a correctness oracle; it is a pre-existing
codegen bug that the segfault had been hiding.

commits.subject: fix(compiler): three ESM/codegen bugs surfaced by the module fixtures
commits.body:
Found while diagnosing test/modules/run.sh failures (t11_colord,
t12_tinycolor). All three are engine bugs, each verified against node
with a minimal repro.

1. hoist_decls swallowed the function body's closing brace.

   The `var` declarator loop consumed the token after a bare final
   declarator without pushing it back when it was not a comma. For an
   unterminated `var` after a return (`function f(){ return x; var t }`)
   that token IS the body's `}`, so brace_depth never returned to 0 and
   the pre-scan ran on past the end of the function, hoisting a sibling
   function's locals into it. In colord this declared a bogus local `h`
   inside `c`, shadowing the module-level `h` helper and making
   `c.toHsl()` throw "undefined is not a function".

2. An assignment expression returned the target local's own register
   without flagging it as a live local.

   binary_expr already guards against using a live local's home register
   as an operator destination, but the guard reads last_was_local_var,
   which the simple- and compound-assignment paths never set. So
   `(u = 45) > 0` emitted `GT r0 = r0, r2` straight into u's slot: u
   read back as `true` instead of 45. Set the flag (and return directly)
   in exactly the two paths that hand back the variable's home register.

3. intern_slot_name returned an unpinned string's bytes.

   The string table holds only a weak reference, so an interned name
   that appears nowhere else sits at refcount 1 and is freed — and its
   bytes zeroed — when that reference drops, leaving the module's
   import/export metadata pointing at reclaimed memory. The alias in
   `export { x as y }` is exactly such a name, so tinycolor's
   `export { tinycolor as default }` registered an export named
   "\0\0\0\0\0\0\0" and `import tinycolor from ...` bound undefined.
   Pin the string, matching how builtin strings are kept alive.

commits.subject: Merge activation_begin(): initialize pooled pointer fields at every push
commits.body:
Activation structs live in a depth-indexed pool and are reused without
zeroing, so a raw pointer field is only safe as a borrow if EVERY push
site writes it. Four sites never wrote async_promise: the getter-invoke
push in vm_core.c3, both setter-invoke pushes in vm_property.c3, and the
generator-resume push in vm_calls.c3. vm_core.c3:95 marks that field
unguarded during GC, and the activation_count bound does not help
because the stale slot sits within the live range — mark_hobject then
writes set_reachable() into freed memory and drains its recycled
prototype and property words.

This was LIVE, not latent: a plain-call frame reusing a slot last held
by an async frame aborts in Heap.sweep with
BUG_IN_CLIENT_OF_LIBMALLOC_POINTER_BEING_FREED_WAS_NOT_ALLOCATED.
test/act_pooled_ptr_fields.js aborts 3/3 on main (SIGABRT, rc=134) and
passes 3/3 here.

Introduce activation_begin() so all pushes clear async_promise,
async_gen_state, new_target, max_heap_reg and caller_valstack_top from
one place, foreclosing the class rather than patching instances. The
fast call path keeps hand-written init, with a comment, because it
publishes to GC only after the frame is built.

Also corrects the field's doc: async_promise is a BORROW, not an owned
reference — no push increfs and no pop decrefs it; the promise is rooted
by the caller's result register and the microtask reactions. Adding a
release would have been a UAF.

commits.subject: fix(vm): initialize the async_promise borrow at every activation push
commits.body:
Activation.async_promise is a BORROW, not a hold: no push site increfs into
the slot and no pop site decrefs out of it. What keeps the promise alive is
the caller's result register (an owning set_object store) plus the reaction
closures on the microtask queue.

Every FUNCTIONAL read of the field is gated on ACT_FLAG_ASYNC, so a stale
value is harmless to the async machinery. mark_activation_fields() is the
exception: it marks the raw pointer on every GC for every activation below
activation_count, with no flag guard at all. Three push sites never wrote
the field — the getter-invoke path (vm_core.c3) and both setter-invoke
paths (vm_property.c3) — so a getter or setter landing on a slot last
occupied by a settled async function inherited a freed HObject*. Marking it
writes set_reachable() INTO FREED MEMORY and then drains the object's
recycled prototype/property words as live references; sweep() then free()s
a pointer it never allocated.

This is live, not latent. test/act_pooled_ptr_fields.js aborts 5/5 with
"pointer being freed was not allocated" inside Heap.sweep on the unfixed
build and passes 5/5 with the fix. Neither half reproduces alone: an
async-only or getter-only version of the same loop exits cleanly.

Rather than patch the three instances, funnel the pooled pushes through a
new activation_begin() helper that clears async_promise, async_gen_state
and new_target together — the doc comment added for async_gen_state in
0758c5fe already told callers to do this, but the helper did not exist.
Six of the seven pooled push sites now use it. The seventh (the fast call
path in vm_calls.c3) cannot: it publishes the slot to the GC only after the
frame is fully built, so it repeats the initialization by hand with a
comment tying the two together.

The remaining raw pointer fields are safe: func/parent/var_env/lex_env/cat/
curr_pc/bottom/retval and this_binding are written at every push site
(verified mechanically). new_target is unwritten by five depth-0 entry
frames in vm_execute.c3, but is co-rooted there by the live global binding
of the constructor — latent, and left alone.

commits.subject: Merge strict-only fix: close the sloppy hole in dynamic Function bodies
commits.body:
AGENTS.md documents a strict-only engine with a single execution mode
and no is_strict flag to branch on, but compile_function's force_strict
escape hatch left dynamic Function/GeneratorFunction/AsyncFunction
bodies sloppy. Two behaviours leaked through: implicit globals and
unqualified delete. (with, legacy octal and arguments.callee were
already rejected.)

Remove force_strict and the ctx.is_strict field, and drop the four dead
is_strict() guards in vm_property.c3.

The subtlety: is_strict was also the sole driver of ES5 10.4.3
this-substitution at five VM sites, so deleting it outright would have
compiled cleanly while silently regressing new Function('return this')()
to undefined — breaking the UMD global-detection idiom. FuncFlags bit 22
is therefore repurposed to subst_global_this rather than removed, which
forced every use site to surface at compile time. this-substitution is
not a strictness distinction; AGENTS.md now says so.

Also fixes a pre-existing spec violation found on the way: delete of a
function-local resolving to a register returned true instead of being a
SyntaxError, because it set last_was_local_var rather than
last_was_getvar and missed the IdentifierReference rejection. That was
wrong in ordinary code too, not just dynamic Function bodies.

Triage: no test changed result in either direction. Phases 3/5/7/8/24
per-test logs diffed with comm, not eyeballed — identical PASS sets,
21231 pass / 0 fail. No skip-list entries needed. Local suite 253/0;
test/strict_only_dynamic_function.js is 26/0 here and fails on main.

Note for cherry-picking: compile_function's 4th argument inverted
meaning from force_strict to dynamic, so (.., true, false) became
(.., true, true).

commits.subject: fix(compiler): close the sloppy-mode hole in dynamic Function bodies
commits.body:
compile_function's `force_strict=false` escape hatch left bodies built by
the Function / GeneratorFunction / AsyncFunction constructors compiling
sloppy, so implicit globals silently worked inside them — the single
remaining hole in the strict-only design (AGENTS.md "Strict-Only Mode").

Removed the parameter. The `is_strict` bit was doing double duty: it
gated sloppy syntax AND was the sole mechanism keeping the ubiquitous UMD
idiom `Function('return this')()` yielding the global object. Those are
separate rules, so bit 22 is repurposed into `subst_global_this` — set
only on dynamic bodies, cleared by a "use strict" directive, and
deliberately not inherited by nested functions. Renaming rather than
deleting the bit forced every use site to surface, including the
this-substitution sites in vm_calls/vm_execute that the runtime flag was
quietly driving.

With nothing left compiling sloppy, the `is_strict()` guards in
vm_property (module-namespace [[Set]]/[[Delete]], get-only accessors) and
the two implicit-global checks in vm_execute become unconditional.
`eval_source_is_strict` is untouched: per AGENTS.md it is orthogonal.

Also fixes an adjacent pre-existing bug found while verifying: `delete
<local>` returned true even in ordinary code. A name resolved to a
register sets `last_was_local_var`, not `last_was_getvar`, so it missed
the IdentifierReference rejection and fell through to the "not a
Reference" branch that unconditionally emits true.

commits.subject: Merge async object-lifetime fixes: three distinct GC bugs
commits.body:
Chasing a report of a promise callback silently never firing turned up
three independent object-lifetime bugs in the async subsystem, all GC
timing bugs that need a long enough promise chain for a collection to
land inside the async machinery.

1. Double free of a GeneratorState. hobject_free decided ownership by
   reading gs.is_async_gen out of a struct the same single-pass sweep
   had already freed. Replaced the two divergent free paths with
   gs_acquire/gs_release so the holder count is the only ownership
   signal, and initialized the Activation.async_gen_state BORROW at the
   four push sites that never wrote it (activation slots are pooled and
   reused without zeroing, and vm_complete_gen_on_unwind writes through
   the field).

2. Value corruption. async_gen_dequeue returned the in-flight request by
   value, leaving its promise unrooted between dequeue and settle; it
   was swept and its slot recycled, so a chain read back [object Object]
   where it had stored 0. Root the request, its value, and the generator
   instance back-edge.

3. Swept callee. native_frame_depth-- before call_fn stripped the
   async-resume wrapper's temproot mid-dispatch. Cache the wrapper on
   the GeneratorState instead.

Also: gs_release now takes the heap explicitly rather than reading a
global cleared before Heap.destroy's free walk, which made it free
heap-allocated memory with mem::free under an embedder allocator.

Verified on release builds against identical inputs — main corrupts
([object Object]1111...) and silently drops a 100-deep chain's final
callback; both correct after. test/async_gen_gc_lifetime.js is 26/26
here and produces no output at all on main. test262 phases 24/8/7:
1231/0, 2777/0, 1208/0, unchanged.

commits.subject: fix(async): stop the async-resume wrapper being swept mid-call
commits.body:
builtin_async_resume / builtin_async_reject built a fresh callable
HObject to re-enter the suspended body, held it in a C3 local, and then
did:

    ctx.heap.native_frame_depth--;
    ctx.heap.call_fn(ctx.vm, func_tv, ...);

The decrement is correct in itself — the resumed body is a full VM
execution, not a nested builtin frame, and leaving the depth raised
would suppress temproot clearing and string sweeping for its entire
duration. But that depth is exactly what protects the wrapper:
mark_and_sweep computes `clear_temproots = safepoint && depth == 0`, and
the wrapper is reachable from nothing else. A safepoint GC inside the
call therefore cleared its temproot and swept the object the VM was
still dispatching through — a use-after-free of the callee itself,
surfacing as HObject.get_shape <- find_prop_idx <- resolve_call_var.

Instrumenting the sweep to flag frees of the in-flight wrapper: 112
occurrences on the old code, 0 after this change, on a 200-iteration
await-with-allocation-churn workload.

The wrapper is per-suspended-body and fully derivable from the
GeneratorState, so cache it there. mark_generator_state already marks
the state, which makes the wrapper a real root instead of a temproot
racing the collector, and removes one allocation per resume. The cached
object's var_env/lex_env are refreshed on every use, since the body's
environments move with each suspension.

Latent without ASAN: on a release build the recycled memory usually
still looks callable, so the corrupted read produced correct output.

commits.subject: fix(async): root an async generator's in-flight request and instance
commits.body:
Two GC-lifetime holes let a live async generator be swept mid-flight.
Both need the collector to fire inside a narrow window, so they only
surfaced once a promise chain was long enough to move the GC trigger
(which scales with live-object count) into that window — hence the
"needs an async generator AND a ~100+ deep chain" shape of the report.

1. The in-flight request was unrooted. async_gen_dequeue returned the
   request struct BY VALUE, so between the dequeue and the settle the
   request's promise and completion value lived only in a C3 local. The
   mark phase cannot see those, so the next allocation could sweep the
   very promise the drain was about to settle. Its slot was then recycled
   into a fresh promise, and the chain read an unrelated value back:
   Promise.resolve(0) observed as [object Object], with v+1 turning the
   rest of the chain into string concatenation. The dequeue now hands the
   promise and value to gs.ag_current_request / gs.ag_current_value, which
   mark_generator_state marks, so ownership is never in a bare local.

2. The generator instance had no root of its own. `g().next()` drops the
   instance on the same line; from then on the only path to the state is a
   reaction closure on the awaited promise. Marking a state now also marks
   its instance through the new gs.gen_obj back-edge, so servicing a
   request cannot free the object servicing it.

Also fixes two latent defects found while auditing the same machinery:

- MARK PHASE: the ASYNC_GEN_RETURN and YRET closure pairs parked a
  GeneratorState* in func.var_env WITHOUT setting is_async_state. That
  flag is what tells mark_hobject the field is not an EnvRecord, so the
  collector walked it as one and marked whatever sat at the EnvRecord
  .bindings offset — in a GeneratorState that is `func`, a
  CompiledFunction*, marked as if it were an HObject. is_async_state is
  now set at all 8 sites that store a state there, making the flag an
  exact discriminator for "var_env holds a GeneratorState".

- CROSS-ALLOCATOR FREE: gs_release inferred its allocator from the
  _active_heap global, which Heap.destroy and Heap.reset clear before
  their free walks — so teardown released a state allocated from the
  heap's allocator back to libc. Benign under the default malloc
  allocator, a real cross-allocator free under an embedder's. The heap is
  now passed explicitly, with a separate flag for "skip the decref pass
  because we are tearing down".

test/async_gen_gc_lifetime.js covers all of it: depth sweep across the
old crash/corruption boundary, abandoned and partially-drained
generators, concurrent for-await consumers, and return()/throw() on
suspended generators. It reports 26/26 identically on node v24. Before
this change it produces no output at all on the same binary.

commits.subject: fix(vm): initialize the async_gen_state borrow at every activation push
commits.body:
Activation.async_gen_state is a BORROW of a GeneratorState: it is
identity-compared during the YIELD parent walk (vm_generators.c3) and
nulled without any release on unwind (vm_throw.c3). That is sound only
because the frame is popped before the generator's own holders can free
the state.

But vm.activations[] is a pool reused WITHOUT zeroing, and four push
sites never wrote the field: the getter invoke path (vm_core.c3), both
setter invoke paths (vm_property.c3), and the constructor path
(vm_calls.c3). A plain call landing on a slot last occupied by a
generator body at the same depth inherited that generator's stale
pointer. vm_complete_gen_on_unwind guards only `!= null` before doing
`gs.state = GEN_COMPLETED`, so an uncaught throw through such a frame
writes through a pointer that may already be freed.

The fast call path in vm_calls.c3 already had this initialization, with
a comment describing exactly this hazard; the other four were simply
missed. Bring them in line and state the contract on the field itself so
the next push site has to confront it.

commits.subject: fix: triage six failing local tests — 3 engine bugs, 5 stale tests
commits.body:

commits.subject: fix(compile): for-head let/const no longer counts as block-level lexical binding
commits.body:
function f() { var y; for (let y in {}) {} } was rejected as a duplicate
declaration because the block pre-scan collected let-names inside the
for's parens (parens don't bump brace_depth) and then the lex-vs-var
check matched them against the function-level var. A for-statement's
LexicalDeclaration binds in the for's own declarative environment
(ES2024 §14.7.4/§14.7.5), not in the enclosing block.

Gate the for-head names out of the block and switch pre-scans by
tracking paren_depth and only collecting let/const at paren_depth == 0.
In valid code a let/const keyword at top-level paren depth can only be
a for-head.

The matching for-head BoundNames vs body VarDeclaredNames early error
(ES2024 §13.7.4.1/§13.7.5.13) was previously covered by the block
pre-scan conflict; once the for-head names stop being collected, the
block scan no longer fires. Add a parse-time check in
check_var_lex_conflict() that walks scope_stack at every true var
declaration site (var statements, for-head var declarations, var
destructure heads) and rejects a var whose name collides with a
let/const in scope. walk the whole stack (past block markers) so
nested-block vars still count toward the enclosing Statement; non-var
kinds and call sites outside true declarations (catch params, function
declarations) are unchanged.

Probes match node's oracle exactly across legal and illegal cases
(blocks, switch, do-while, block-fn, catch, nested var-in-for-head
forms, multi-form destructure). Rosetta 100/100, golden 10/10, gate
2/2 zero-fail (45,617 pass / 0 fail / 0 CE).

commits.subject: fix(async): refcount GeneratorState across its HObject holders
commits.body:
A GeneratorState is referenced by the GENERATOR instance and by every
is_async_state reaction closure that parks the pointer in func.var_env.
Ownership was decided by reading a gs field, so during a sweep that tears
down several holders in one pass the first free recycled the struct and
the next holder read back whatever landed there — a use-after-free that
surfaced as an async reaction silently never running.

Add gs_acquire/gs_release so the holder count is the only ownership
signal and the last teardown, in whatever order sweep visits them, frees.

Fixes the silent drop where an async generator plus a >=100-deep promise
chain left the chain's final .then callback unrun.

WIP: a separate value-corruption bug remains — a 400-deep chain plus an
async generator still reads Promise.resolve(0) back as [object Object].

commits.subject: Merge for-in correctness + performance work and local regression coverage
commits.body:
Six fixes found by reviewing the plan 062 batch-1 commits, plus the local
tests that batch shipped without.

Correctness:
- for-in no longer enumerates symbol keys (EnumerateObjectProperties
  yields String keys only); stringifying one used to throw.
- A proxy's non-enumerable own keys now shadow the prototype chain, and
  keys whose [[GetOwnProperty]] reports undefined correctly do not.
- A String object's own non-enumerable length shadows an inherited one.
- NEW_OBJ and the two Vm.execute entry points clear the pooled
  activation's async fields instead of inheriting stale pointers.
- Corrected the async-return refcount comments: set_object increfs, so
  the promise alias is owned; the old text invited a double-free.

Performance: the group F shadowing rule was implemented as an eager
pre-pass per chain level over a linearly scanned seen set, making for-in
quadratic in the chain's total property count (4.3x on a deep chain, 1.6x
on a plain object literal). Replaced with a lazy shadow probe and a
hashed seen set; now faster than before group F landed.

Tests: 347 local assertions across four files, each verified to fail when
its fix is reverted. test262 phases 3/7/23/24: 10304 pass, 0 fail.

commits.subject: perf(for-in): allocate the seen-set backing array on first insert
commits.body:
A single-level enumeration, or one whose keys all come from the last
chain level, never inserts anything into the seen set, so the 512-byte
allocation up front was pure waste. forin_ensure_cap now allocates on
first use.

commits.subject: fix(vm): for-in must not enumerate symbol-keyed properties
commits.body:
EnumerateObjectProperties (ES2024 14.7.5.9) yields only keys of type
String. collect_forin_keys had a "Phase 3" loop that explicitly added
enumerable symbol keys, so `for (var k in o)` yielded symbols. Beyond
the wrong key list this was a hard failure: any use of the loop
variable in string context threw "Cannot convert a Symbol value to a
string", so a single symbol-keyed property broke an otherwise valid
for-in.

The loop dates to 02884b72, which applied the OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys
ordering rule (integers, then strings, then symbols) to for-in. That
ordering governs [[OwnPropertyKeys]], not EnumerateObjectProperties,
which filters to String keys before any ordering applies.

The loop served no shadowing purpose: symbol keys are a distinct
HString flavor and can never be pointer-equal to a string key, so they
can neither shadow nor be shadowed. The Phase 2 pre-pass already
excluded symbols from `seen`, so only enumerable symbols ever entered
it — via the yield path being removed here.

The other key sources were already correct and are unchanged: the
Proxy path filters symbols in proxy_filtered_own_keys (mode 0) and the
module-namespace path has its own is_symbol() guard. Object.keys,
JSON.stringify, Object.assign and spread use separate own-keys
collection and still see symbols as required.

test/forin.js: 8 -> 21 assertions, covering enumerable/non-enumerable
symbols, prototype-chain symbols, well-known symbols, a Proxy whose
ownKeys trap returns symbols, and that the own-keys paths are
unaffected. Every expectation cross-checked against node.

test262 unchanged: phase 7 1208/1208, phase 3 7603/7603,
phase 23 (Proxy) 262/262, 0 fails each.

The lazy shadow probe and its eager deep-chain fallback both exempted a
String object's own `length`, so an inherited enumerable `length` was
still yielded. `length` is non-enumerable, so EnumerateObjectProperties
records it as visited and it must suppress the prototype's.

Resolves the overlap between the seen-set rework and the proxy/String

commits.subject: fix(for-in): size the seen-set hash index to a power of two
commits.body:
The index built at promotion was FORIN_SEEN_HASH_THRESHOLD * 4 = 48
slots, so `index_mask` was 47 and `(slot + 1) & 47` never visited every
slot. A probe for an absent key could then cycle forever instead of
landing on an empty slot — an infinite loop as soon as one chain level
pushed the seen set past the promotion threshold and a later level
looked up a key that missed.

Give the initial index its own power-of-two constant and document the
requirement on reindex. Doubling on growth already preserved it.

Adds for-in coverage for prototype-chain shadowing (including past the
lazily-probed level window) and for a two-level enumeration large enough
to promote the index and then probe it with misses.

commits.subject: perf(for-in): lazy shadow probe + hashed seen set
commits.body:
collect_forin_keys was quadratic in the total own-property count of the
whole prototype chain: the seen set was a linearly scanned array, and the
non-enumerable pre-passes added every own non-enumerable key of every
level to it — hundreds of entries for a class instance or a deep chain,
none of which are ever yielded.

Two changes:

- Replace the pre-passes with a lazy probe. The shadowing rule (a
  non-enumerable own key suppresses a same-named enumerable prototype
  key) is now checked when a key is about to be yielded, by testing the
  already-walked levels with find_prop_idx, instead of eagerly copying
  every non-enumerable key into the seen set. Prototypes are almost
  entirely non-enumerable methods, so the eager work was pure waste.
  Chains deeper than FORIN_NEARER_MAX fall back to eager recording.

- Give the seen set an open-addressing index keyed on the interned
  string's precomputed hash once it grows past a small threshold, so
  membership is O(1) rather than a linear scan.

The final chain level now also skips the seen-set inserts entirely:
nothing above it is left to shadow.

commits.subject: fix(vm): non-enumerable own keys shadow the prototype in proxy/String for-in
commits.body:
EnumerateObjectProperties records every own key it visits — including
non-enumerable ones — as already-seen, so a same-named enumerable property
further up the prototype chain is suppressed. Two own-key sources missed
this rule.

Proxies: the for-in branch used proxy_filtered_own_keys(mode 0), which
drops non-enumerable keys before returning, so they never reached the
`seen` set. Add proxy_partitioned_own_keys, which keeps them in a second
partition of the same buffer instead of discarding them. It reuses the
[[GetOwnProperty]] call the filter already makes, so trap invocation
count and order are unchanged; proxy_filtered_own_keys becomes a wrapper
and its three other callers are untouched. Keys whose [[GetOwnProperty]]
returns undefined land in neither partition — the spec marks a key
visited only "if desc is not undefined", so an absent key must not shadow.

String objects: the pre-pass skipped the own non-enumerable `length`, so
it was neither yielded nor marked, letting a prototype `length` leak
through. Drop the skip. The matching skip in the yield loop was dead —
`length` is non-configurable and non-enumerable, so the loop's enumerable
check already excluded it — and is removed too.

Other own-key sources were audited against node and need no change:
typed array indices, dense array elements, string indices and module
namespace exports are all enumerable by spec, and the non-enumerable
Array `length`, arguments `callee`/`length` and Function `length`/`name`
are ordinary named props already covered by the existing pre-pass.

acts as the pin"; in fact TVal.set_object increfs, so val holds a

commits.subject: fix(for-in): restore env writes for function-nested lexical iter-vars
commits.body:
A 'for (let p in obj) body' inside a function whose body reads 'p' was
throwing ReferenceError 'p is not defined'.  Root cause: the for-in
head (statements.c3 for_statement) marks the freshly-declared iter-var
scope entry as is_captured=true so resolve_var forces body reads
through GETVAR, but the matching has_captured_local=true flip was
missing.  Without it the register-resident-locals elision in
CompilerContext.finish() saw elide_ok=true (no closures / no captured
locals / etc.) and NOP'd the per-iteration PUTLEX and the head INITTZ.
The body's GETVAR then walked the (empty) lex_env chain and threw.

The fix is a single line at statements.c3:2339 (plus a comment block
documenting the invariant at context.c3:1118): whenever is_captured
is forced on a scope entry post-declare, has_captured_local must be
flipped in the same breath so the elide gate agrees with resolve_var's
read-redirection gate.
